```js
export async function liveChannels({ categoryId, cursor }) {
  const page = await api("/canales?categoria=" + encodeURIComponent(categoryId) + (cursor ? "&pagina=" + encodeURIComponent(cursor) : ""));
  return {
    items: page.canales.map((c) => ({ id: c.id, title: c.nombre, categoryId, ref: c.id, logo: c.logo, number: c.numero })),
    next: page.siguiente || undefined,
  };
}

// Called on every play, and again when the stream is cut: always a fresh token.
export async function resolve(ref) {
  const s = await api("/firmar/" + encodeURIComponent(ref)); // { url: "https://cdn.example.com/…?token=…" }
  return { url: s.url, mime: "application/vnd.apple.mpegurl" };
}
```

```
node sdk/run.mjs . --config token=... live channels noticias
```

### 3. Mixed { #recipe-mixed }

Your own "Destacados" category with inline `stream` items (they play with no call to
your plugin, so zapping through them is instant), plus the provider's full list declared with
`resolve: true`: Kino downloads and groups it, and each of its entries plays through your
`resolve(<entry url>)`, which appends a token.

```json
{
  "id": "mi-mezcla", "name": "Mi mezcla", "version": "1.0.0", "apiVersion": 3, "entry": "plugin.js",
  "hosts": ["api.example.com", "live.example.com", "listas.example.com"],
  "capabilities": ["home", "resolve", "channels"]
}
```

```js
// Your own featured channels: inline streams, played with no call to the plugin (fast zapping).
const DESTACADOS = [
  { id: "noticias24", title: "Noticias 24", number: 1, url: "https://live.example.com/noticias24/index.m3u8" },
  { id: "deportes", title: "Deportes", number: 2, url: "https://live.example.com/deportes/index.m3u8" },
];

export async function home() {
  return [];
}

export async function liveCategories() {
  return [
    { id: "destacados", title: "Destacados" },
    // The provider's full list: Kino downloads and groups it; each entry plays through resolve().
    {
      playlist: {
        url: "https://listas.example.com/todos.m3u",
        format: "m3u",
        epg: { url: "https://listas.example.com/guia.xml.gz", format: "xmltv" },
        resolve: true,
      },
    },
  ];
}

export async function liveChannels({ categoryId }) {
  if (categoryId !== "destacados") return { items: [] };
  return {
    items: DESTACADOS.map((c) => ({ id: c.id, title: c.title, number: c.number, categoryId, stream: { url: c.url } })),
  };
}

// Only the list's entries get here (resolve: true), with the entry's URL as the ref.
export async function resolve(url) {
  const r = await kino.fetch("https://api.example.com/token");
  if (!r.ok) throw kino.error("unavailable", "no hay token");
  const { token } = r.json();
  return { url: url + (url.includes("?") ? "&" : "?") + "token=" + encodeURIComponent(token) };
}
```

The list's streams must be on your `hosts` here (`live.example.com`), since this manifest does not
declare `"liveStreamHosts": "any"`; `live categories` counts the entries that are not as discarded.

```
node sdk/run.mjs . live categories
node sdk/run.mjs . live channels destacados
```

The published demo [Tu servidor](cookbook.md#own-server) (1.5.0) uses all three shapes at once
(channels with a `ref`, channels with an inline `stream`, and an M3U playlist with an XMLTV guide),
plus a second playlist with `resolve: true` whose links need its token, `liveSearch` and paged
`liveChannels` ([The channel functions](#live-contract)), all on the person's own server: see
`liveCategories`, `channel`, `liveChannels`, `liveSearch` and `resolveListEntry` in its
[`plugin.js`](https://github.com/kinotvapp/kino-plugin-own-server/blob/main/plugin.js#L357-L436).


<!-- page: https://kinotvapp.github.io/kino-plugins/en/music/ (docs/music.en.md) -->

# Music and podcasts

From **`"apiVersion": 8` (Kino 0.9.54)** a plugin can offer audio next to (or instead of) video:
albums, playlists and tracks, podcasts, audiobooks and radio shows. This page is the short version;
every rule, with its exact values, is in the contract:
[Music and podcasts](contract.md#music-podcasts).

## The two kinds { #kinds }

| `kind` | What it is | One "episode" is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"music"` | an album, a playlist or a single track | a track |
| `"podcast"` | a show, an audiobook or a radio program | an episode or a chapter |

An audio item goes in `search`, `browse`, `home` rows and your section like any other item. The
optional `artist` field (`music` and `podcast` only, at most 200 characters) is the artist, or the
host or author: the album or podcast page shows it under the title.

## How it plays { #play }

- **With the `episodes` capability**, Kino calls `episodes(ref)` for **every** `music` and `podcast`
  item: the tracks of an album, the chapters of an audiobook, the episodes of a show, in your order.
  It must answer for each audio ref, even a single track (one entry): there is no per-item way to
  skip it. Each entry's `ref` goes to `resolve`.
- **Without `episodes`**, the item's own `ref` goes straight to `resolve` and plays as one track.
- The `Stream` is a normal one: progressive audio (MP3, M4A, AAC, OGG) or an HLS/DASH manifest.

## Before you declare 8 { #version }

- An older Kino refuses an apiVersion 8 plugin ("Este plugin necesita una versión más nueva de
  Kino"): declare 8 only when you return audio items or export [`details`](contract.md#details).
- Below apiVersion 8 a `music` or `podcast` item is dropped (with a line in the log); the rest of the
  answer stays.
- From apiVersion 8, `details` is a reserved export name: never export a helper called `details`.

## The reference audio plugin { #reference }

[**Internet Archive Audio**](https://github.com/kinotvapp/kino-plugin-archive-audio)
(`kinotvapp/kino-plugin-archive-audio`, apiVersion 8): free music, live concerts, audiobooks and
old-time radio from archive.org. Its `episodes` answers for every album, audiobook and show (a single
78 rpm side included), and `resolve` offers each audio format as a labelled lazy copy. Start from it
for an audio plugin; see also [Example plugins](examples.md).

What the person gets in Kino 0.9.54 (square covers, the album or podcast page, the audio player,
"Seguir escuchando", downloads and cast) is listed in
[the contract](contract.md#music-podcasts).


<!-- page: https://kinotvapp.github.io/kino-plugins/en/catalog/ (docs/catalog.en.md) -->

# Catalog and large storage (`catalog`, `storageLarge`, apiVersion 13) { #catalog }

!!! note "Available from Kino 0.9.74"
    apiVersion 13 arrives in Kino 0.9.74, together with apiVersion 12. Every Kino before 0.9.74 refuses a manifest with
    `"apiVersion": 13` ("Este plugin necesita una versión más nueva de Kino").

A plugin whose source is a big library (every video of a Telegram channel, a site's whole archive, a self-hosted media
folder) needs to find things in thousands of records. Keeping them in `kino.storage` and filtering in JavaScript means
loading the whole list into your plugin's 64 MB of QuickJS memory on every search. `kino.catalog` keeps them in a SQLite
database that Kino owns for your plugin, and searches them there: your code only ever holds the page it asked for.

## Which store to use { #which-store }

| You keep | Use | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Settings, a token, a cursor, a few small JSON values | `kino.storage` | 256 KB, synchronous, carried by a password-protected backup |
| A few big opaque blobs you read whole (a cached index file, a key bundle) | `kino.storage` with [`storageLarge`](#storage-large) | 16 MB, one file per value, device-only |
| Thousands of records you search, sort and page through | `kino.catalog` | up to 100,000 items in a 64 MiB file (about 670 bytes per item on average, so keep `data` small), searched by Kino, never loaded whole |

## Declaring it { #declare }

```json
"apiVersion": 13,
"capabilities": ["search", "resolve", "catalog"]
```

`catalog` is declarative: nothing to export, no consent line and no approval (it is room on this device, not reach to
anyone). An older Kino refuses the manifest ("Este plugin necesita una versión más nueva de Kino"), and a manifest below `apiVersion` 13 is
refused with "The \"catalog\" capability needs apiVersion 13". A plugin that does not declare it has no `kino.catalog` at
all (`typeof kino.catalog === "undefined"`), and neither does `sign()`.

## The operations { #operations }

Every operation is `async` (`await` it) and answers plain JSON values. All six, with their exact shapes:

| Call | Takes | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kino.catalog.upsert(items)` | an array of at most 500 `{ id, title, sort?, data? }` | `{ count }`: how many items were written |
| `kino.catalog.search(options?)` | `{ q?, limit?, offset?, order? }`: `q` default `""` (everything), `limit` default 50 (1 to 100), `offset` default 0 (0 to 1,000,000), `order` default `"newest"` | `{ items, total }`: one page of `{ id, title, sort, data }` and the count of every match |
| `kino.catalog.get(ids)` | an array of at most 500 ids | the items found, in the order asked; missing ids are skipped, a repeated id comes once |
| `kino.catalog.remove(ids)` | an array of at most 500 ids | `{ count }`: how many were there and are now gone |
| `kino.catalog.clear()` | nothing | nothing: every item is gone and Kino deletes the file |
| `kino.catalog.count()` | nothing | the number of items |

A whole mini-plugin, runnable as it is (the Node kit's tests run this very code against a fake source). It indexes a
source that pages its videos newest first, a few pages per Home call so no call runs past its time limit; answers
`search` from the catalog only; drops a video the source deleted when someone tries to play it; and starts over once a
week (which also drops what the source deleted) or when the catalog comes back empty after a restore or a reset.

```js
// kino-plugin.json (the parts that matter): {"apiVersion": 13, "capabilities": ["home", "search", "resolve", "catalog"], "hosts": ["api.example.org"]}
const BATCH = 500;                         // maxUpsertBatch
const MAX_TITLE = 300;                     // maxTitleChars
const PAGES_PER_CALL = 3;                  // a few source pages per Home call
const ID_RE = /^[A-Za-z0-9._~-]{1,120}$/;  // fits a Kino Item id (128 characters) once prefixed with "v"
const WEEK_MS = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

async function sourcePage(cursor) {
  const url = "https://api.example.org/videos" + (cursor ? "?after=" + encodeURIComponent(cursor) : "");
  const r = await kino.fetch(url);
  if (!r.ok) throw kino.error("unavailable", "the source answered " + r.status);
  return r.json(); // { videos: [{ id, caption, date, file, poster }], next }, newest first
}

// At most `max` characters (JavaScript's length, as Kino counts them), never cutting a character in two.
function clip(text, max) {
  let t = String(text).slice(0, max);
  if (/[\uD800-\uDBFF]$/.test(t)) t = t.slice(0, -1);
  return t;
}

// One source video as a catalog item, or null to skip it. A caption can be missing or far longer than 300 characters,
// and one bad item would refuse its whole batch of 500: the title is never empty and always fits, the id fits Kino's
// Item id, and `data` holds only small fields.
function toItem(v) {
  const id = String(v.id);
  if (!ID_RE.test(id)) return null;
  const title = clip(String(v.caption || "").replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim(), MAX_TITLE) || "Video " + id;
  return {
    id,
    title,
    sort: Number.isSafeInteger(v.date) ? v.date : 0, // "newest" = the biggest date first
    data: { file: clip(v.file || "", 200), poster: v.poster ? clip(v.poster, 500) : null },
  };
}

async function upsertAll(items) {
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i += BATCH) await kino.catalog.upsert(items.slice(i, i + BATCH));
}

// The catalog stays on this device, but kino.storage travels in a backup: after a restore, on a new device or after a
// "damaged" reset the catalog is empty while the markers still say it was indexed. Start over then.
async function forgetIndexIfEmpty() {
  if (kino.storage.get("indexedAt") !== null && (await kino.catalog.count()) === 0) {
    kino.storage.remove("indexedAt");
    kino.storage.remove("cursor");
  }
}

// One step of indexing, from Home (20 s per call), never from search (15 s, and the person is waiting):
// - not complete yet: go on with the full pass where the last step stopped (a cursor in kino.storage);
// - complete: read from the newest video and stop at the first page holding an item already indexed;
// - a week after the last full pass: clear and index again.
async function indexStep() {
  const at = Number(kino.storage.get("indexedAt"));
  if (at && Date.now() - at > WEEK_MS) {
    await kino.catalog.clear();
    kino.storage.remove("indexedAt");
    kino.storage.remove("cursor");
  }
  const complete = kino.storage.get("indexedAt") !== null;
  let cursor = complete ? null : kino.storage.get("cursor");
  for (let i = 0; i < PAGES_PER_CALL; i++) {
    const page = await sourcePage(cursor);
    const items = page.videos.map(toItem).filter((it) => it !== null);
    const known = complete && items.length > 0 && (await kino.catalog.get(items.slice(0, BATCH).map((it) => it.id))).length > 0;
    await upsertAll(items);
    if (known || !page.next) {
      if (!complete) {
        kino.storage.set("indexedAt", String(Date.now()));
        kino.storage.remove("cursor");
      }
      return;
    }
    cursor = page.next;
    if (!complete) kino.storage.set("cursor", cursor);
  }
}

const toKinoItem = (it) => ({ id: "v" + it.id, ref: it.id, title: it.title, kind: "movie", poster: (it.data && it.data.poster) || undefined });

export async function home() {
  try {
    await forgetIndexIfEmpty();
    await indexStep();
  } catch (e) {
    // The source or the catalog is unavailable right now: show what the catalog already has; the next Home goes on.
    if (e.code !== "unavailable") throw e;
    kino.log("indexing paused: " + e.message);
  }
  const newest = await kino.catalog.search({ limit: 20 });
  return [{ id: "newest", title: "Newest", items: newest.items.map(toKinoItem) }];
}

export async function search(query) {
  // The catalog only: cheap enough for every keystroke, and never the network.
  const page = await kino.catalog.search({ q: String(query.q || "").slice(0, 256), limit: 50 });
  return page.items.map(toKinoItem);
}

export async function resolve(ref) {
  const [item] = await kino.catalog.get([ref]);
  if (!item) throw kino.error("not_found", "no longer in the catalog");
  const r = await kino.fetch("https://api.example.org/files/" + encodeURIComponent(item.data.file));
  if (r.status === 404) {
    await kino.catalog.remove([ref]); // the source deleted it: drop it now, not at the weekly rebuild
    throw kino.error("not_found", "the source deleted this video");
  }
  return { url: r.json().url };
}
```

A Kino `Item`'s `id` must match `^[A-Za-z0-9._~-]{1,128}$`; a catalog `id` can be any string of 1 to 128 characters, so
map it when yours has other characters or would pass 128 once prefixed (the example skips such videos; a hash of the id
works too).

## How search matches { #search }

- **Case and accents do not matter.** Kino keeps each title lower-cased with its accents removed (Unicode NFD without
  the combining marks) and does the same to `q`: `"pelicula"`, `"PELÍCULA"` and `"Película"` all find "Película";
  `"nandu"` finds "Ñandú". Control characters other than whitespace (a NUL, an escape code) are dropped from both, so
  `"ab\u0000zz"` and `"abzz"` find the same items.
- **Every word must be there, in any order, as part of the title.** `q` is split on whitespace; each word must appear
  somewhere in the title: `"rojo gato"` and `"gato rojo"` both find "El gato ROJO", and `"gat roj"` finds it too. There
  is no ranking and no fuzzy match: an item either matches or not.
- **`%`, `_` and `\` are plain characters.** They are never wildcards: `"50%"` finds "50% off" and not "50 off";
  `"a_b"` finds "a_b" and not "axb". No query can run anything: there is no SQL on your side at all.
- **Empty, blank or absent `q` lists everything** (in the order asked).
- **Only `title` is searched**, never `id` or `data`. Put every word a person might type in the title.
- **Order.** `"newest"` (the default): `sort` from biggest to smallest; `"oldest"`: smallest first; `"title"`: by the
  title without case or accents, then the title as written, then the id. Ties are always broken by `id`, so the same
  query pages the same way every time.
- **`items` and `total`.** `items` is the page (at most `limit`); `total` is how many items match in all. There is more
  when `offset + items.length < total`.
- **Paging.** `limit` is 1 to 100 (default 50) and `offset` 0 to 1,000,000, whole numbers (`NaN` or `Infinity` is
  `invalid_request`); an `offset` past the end answers no items and the same `total`. `q` is at most 256 characters.

```js
await kino.catalog.search({ q: "gato rojo" });                                  // newest first, 50 at most
await kino.catalog.search({ q: "gato", order: "title", limit: 20, offset: 40 }); // the third page of 20, A to Z
const { total } = await kino.catalog.search({ q: "2001", limit: 1 });            // just the count of matches
```

## The data model { #data-model }

One table, one row per item: `id` (your key, 1 to 128 characters), `title` (at most 300 characters; the only thing
searched), `sort` (a whole number, default 0: a date in milliseconds, a message number, an episode number) and `data`
(an optional plain object whose JSON is at most 4,096 bytes in UTF-8, given back as you stored it). Put in `data` the
few fields you show or need to play (a poster URL, a duration, a file reference), never blobs, pages of HTML or
credentials. `upsert` with an `id` that is already there **replaces the whole item**: a field you leave out is gone
(the `data` too). A batch is one transaction: if any item in it is refused, nothing of it is written, so clean your items
first (as `toItem` does above) rather than sending what the source gave you as it is.

## How many items fit { #how-many }

Two limits hold at once: 100,000 items and a 64 MiB file. 100,000 items fit only when an item
costs at most about 670 bytes of the file on average: its id, its title twice (as written and without case or
accents), its `data`, and the two search indexes. Measured in Kino's tests with a 50-character title: about 370 bytes
with no `data` (100,000 fit, in 37 MB), about 690 bytes with 300 bytes of `data` (about 96,000 fit), about 920 bytes
with 500 bytes (about 72,000), and about 4,850 bytes with 4,000 bytes (about 13,800). Keep `data` small: a file
reference and a poster URL, not a description.

## Limits and errors { #limits }

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Items per plugin | 100,000, if they fit in the file (see "How many items fit") |
| `id` | 1 to 128 characters |
| `title` | at most 300 characters |
| `data` | at most 4,096 bytes of JSON (UTF-8) |
| Items per `upsert`, ids per `get` or `remove` | 500 |
| `search` `limit` | default 50, at most 100 |
| `search` `offset` | at most 1,000,000 |
| `search` `q` | at most 256 characters |
| The database file | at most 64 MiB |

Every refusal is a `KinoError` whose `code` says what to do, and whose message names the limit:

| `code` | When | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `invalid_request` | A wrong shape or type: `upsert` without an array, an item without a string `id` or `title`, a fractional or non-finite `sort`, a `data` that is not an object, a `limit` of 0 or `NaN`, an unknown `order`. | Fix the call; the message says which item (`item 3`) and which field. |
| `too_large` | One value or one batch over its limit: `"kino.catalog.upsert: at most 500 items per call (maxUpsertBatch)"`, `"kino.catalog.upsert: item 0 data is over 4096 bytes as JSON (maxDataBytes)"`, a long `id` or `title`, `"kino.catalog.search: limit is over 100 (maxSearchLimit)"`, an `offset` or `q` over its limit. | Split the batch, shorten the value, ask a smaller page. |
| `limit` | The catalog is full: `"kino.catalog.upsert: the catalog is full (maxItems 100000)"` or `"kino.catalog.upsert: the catalog file is full (maxDbBytes 64 MiB)"`. | Remove items you no longer need (or `clear` and index less, with smaller `data`), then try again. |
| `unavailable` | Kino could not read or write the file right now (the device's storage failed or is full), or the plugin was just removed. When the file was corrupt, Kino deletes it and starts an empty one, and that call says `"kino.catalog: the catalog file was damaged and has been reset to empty; rebuild it"`. A file a newer Kino wrote (after the person went back to an older Kino) says `"kino.catalog: the catalog file was made by a newer Kino"` on every call until you `clear()` it. | Try again later; after "damaged", index again from your source; after "made by a newer Kino", `clear()` (it deletes that file and starts a new one) and index again. |

A refused `upsert` writes nothing of its batch, so retrying a smaller one is safe. Kino never deletes your catalog on an
I/O error: only a file SQLite reports as corrupt is replaced.

## Isolation and privacy { #privacy }

- **One database file per plugin.** Your catalog is `catalog.db` inside your plugin's own data folder, named from your
  plugin's id alone; Kino picks it when it starts your plugin, and no argument you pass can name another plugin or
  another file. No other plugin can read or change your items, and you cannot read theirs.
- **No SQL from plugins, ever.** You only have the six operations above; every value you send is bound as a parameter.
- **It stays on this device: never synced, and excluded from backups.** It is a rebuildable cache of your source. No
  backup carries it, so on another device, after a restore there, or after the person uninstalls and reinstalls your
  plugin, it is empty: check `kino.catalog.count()` (as `forgetIndexIfEmpty` does above) and index again from your source.
- **Uninstalling the plugin deletes the file**, and a call of yours still running at that moment cannot create it again.
- **Credentials do NOT belong here.** Keep tokens and sessions in [sealed secrets](manifest.md#secrets), the
  person's settings or `kino.storage`, never in `data`.

## Performance { #performance }

- Write in batches of up to 500 items: each `upsert` is one transaction, much faster than one call per item.
- Never load the whole catalog into memory to filter it yourself: ask `search` for a page and let Kino do the
  matching. A page is at most 100 items.
- Page through big results with `limit`/`offset` instead of asking everything; read `total` with `limit: 1` when you only
  need the count.
- What it costs: a search reads every title once (a substring match cannot use an index to find words; the indexes
  carry the searched text so the rows themselves are read only for matches) plus the page asked for. Measured in Kino's
  JVM tests on a desktop computer (an Apple Silicon Mac), not on a phone or a TV box: two searches with their totals over
  50,000 items took 68 to 86 ms, with no `data` and with 500 bytes or 4,000 bytes of `data` per item alike. A phone or
  a 1 GB TV box is slower by a factor nobody has measured yet: test your plugin on the slowest device you support.
- Index from Home or a refresh of your own, a few source pages per call, never inside `search`: every call has its own
  time limit (15 s for `search`, 20 s for `home`) and the person waits for a search.

## Recipes { #recipes }

- **Index a remote library incrementally.** As `indexStep` above: a full pass the first time, a few pages per call with
  a cursor in `kino.storage`; after that, read from the newest item and stop at the first page holding an item already
  indexed (`kino.catalog.get` answers it), `upsert`ing each page as you go. A full rebuild (`clear` then index) is for a
  schedule (once a week drops what the source deleted) or when your source changed shape.
- **Search as the person types.** In a "Ver más" page with `scopedSearch`, Kino waits 400 ms after the person stops
  typing before it calls your `search`, and a new query can follow right after: answer each call straight from
  `kino.catalog.search({ q: query.q })`, never from the network. While the catalog is still empty, answer what it has
  (nothing): Home fills it.
- **Say when older items are not loaded yet.** While the full pass is not complete (the `cursor` marker above is still
  there), add an item to your Home row, or a `userMessage` to an empty search, that says the library is still being
  read; drop it once `indexedAt` is set.

## A bigger storage instead: `storageLarge` { #storage-large }

A plugin that indexes a catalog (thousands of videos of a channel, a library it builds from its source) runs out of
256 KB after a few hundred entries. To **search** thousands of records, use [`kino.catalog`](#catalog)
instead: it never loads them into your memory. Declare `storageLarge` and the same `kino.storage` holds **16 MB in total
(16,777,216 bytes: every key and value, UTF-8), at most 2 MB per value (2,097,152 bytes) and at most 1,000 keys of at
most 256 characters**:

```json
"apiVersion": 13,
"capabilities": ["search", "resolve", "storageLarge"]
```

- Same API and the same `ttlMs` rules. Declarative (nothing to export) and no consent line: it is room on the device,
  not reach.
- **Shard the catalog into values of at most about 512 KB** (`catalog:0`, `catalog:1`, ... plus a small key that says
  how many there are). Every string your plugin holds costs QuickJS memory (a 2 MB string is 4 MB of your 64 MB), and
  Kino keeps each value in its own file: a `get` reads one value, a `set` writes one value, so small shards stay fast on
  a 1 GB TV box.
- Going over throws a `KinoError` with `code` `"too_large"`: `"plugin storage full (2 MB per value)"`,
  `"plugin storage full (16 MB)"` when the whole store would pass 16 MB, `"plugin storage full (1000 keys)"`. A key
  longer than 256 characters is `"invalid_request"`. A refused write changes nothing.
- **It is device-only: never synced and NOT in any backup.** A plugin without the capability has its 256 KB
  `kino.storage` carried by a backup with a password; a plugin with `storageLarge` has nothing of its `kino.storage` in
  a backup, and restoring one leaves it empty. Treat it as a cache you rebuild from your source.
- **Declaring `storageLarge` moves your existing keys into that device-only store.** The first call after an update that
  adds it moves everything your plugin had stored (tokens and sessions included) out of the backed-up store, at most
  1,000 keys of at most 256 characters (the rest is dropped). Keep credentials and sessions in
  [sealed secrets](manifest.md#secrets) or the person's settings, or in a plugin that does not declare
  `storageLarge`.
- An update that drops `storageLarge` starts again from an empty 256 KB store (the larger one stays on the device until
  the capability comes back or the plugin is uninstalled).
- An older Kino refuses a manifest with `storageLarge` ("Este plugin necesita una versión más nueva de Kino").


<!-- page: https://kinotvapp.github.io/kino-plugins/en/signed-streams/ (docs/signed-streams.en.md) -->

# Signing every request (`signing`, apiVersion 6)

Some origins want a fresh signature on **every** request: a header that expires in seconds. From
`"apiVersion": 6` (Kino 0.9.50), return `signing: "request"` in the stream, and export `sign`:

```js
export async function resolve(ref, options) {
  const session = await openSession(options?.retry); // a retry says why: "conflict" or "expired"
  return { url: session.playlist, signing: "request", signContext: JSON.stringify({ token: session.token }),
           headers: { "Content-License": session.license } };
}

export async function sign({ url, kind, ref, context }) { // kind: "playlist" | "segment"
  const { token } = JSON.parse(context);
  return { headers: { "Content-Auth": await signatureFor(token, Date.now()) } };
}
```

Kino plays the stream through a local proxy. Before every playlist and segment request it calls
`sign()` and sends its headers, merged over the stream's own `headers`.

!!! note "It is for origins that really require it"
    If your origin accepts a token that lasts minutes, return it in `headers` or the URL and use
    [`expiresInSeconds`](contract.md#stream): simpler, and it does not go through the proxy.

## The rules { #rules }

- **HLS only**: an HLS `mime`, or a `.m3u8` path. No `drm`, no `audioTracks` (subtitles are fine: they
  get the stream's own `headers`, like any stream's subtitles, but are never `sign()`ed). An inline
  `stream` of a `liveChannels` item can't ask for it: a channel that also has a `ref` plays through
  `resolve(ref)` (the inline stream is set aside), and one without a `ref` is dropped. A stream that
  breaks these is refused with `per-request signing only works with HLS video (.m3u8)`, `a video signed
  per request can't carry drm or separate audio tracks` or `a channel signed per request must play
  through resolve()` (the log's detail; the person reads Kino's own line). A signed video can't be
  downloaded: its download ends with `Este contenido no se puede descargar` (Kino 0.9.53 and older:
  `Este video no se puede descargar`).
- **`sign()` runs apart from your other functions** (the "signing lane"), so a slow `home` never delays
  a segment. It gets `kino.crypto`, `kino.secret`, `kino.config`, `kino.html` and `kino.log`, and nothing
  else: `kino.fetch` answers a `host_not_allowed` error ("sign can't use the network"), and
  `kino.storage`, `kino.cookies` and `kino.sleep` fail with the code `not_allowed` and "sign() can't use
  kino.storage: whatever you need must come in signContext" (likewise for the others). It also can't
  see anything the main runtime holds in memory (not even the private keys of
  [`generateKeyPair`](kino-api.md#key-pairs)).
- What it needs travels in `context`, the `signContext` your `resolve()` returned (a string of up to
  4096 characters; a longer or non-string one refuses the stream with `the "signContext" value is
  not valid`). A `kino.secret()` marker means nothing there (a marker only works in the runtime that made
  it): call `kino.secret()` inside `sign()` itself; a `signContext` carrying one is refused with
  "signContext can't carry a kino.secret(): call it inside sign()".
- A stream asking for `signing: "request"` from a plugin that doesn't export `sign` is refused with "the
  plugin asks to sign the video but doesn't export sign()".
- **1.5 s per call** (3 s counting its wait). A slow answer counts as a failed signature.
- Answer `{ headers }`, filtered like a stream's `headers` (same names and size rules). A value
  containing a `kino.secret()` marker is refused ("sign can't return sealed data"): a marker is
  only good inside `kino.crypto`, so compute the header there.
- Three failed signatures in a row stop the video.
- Below apiVersion 6, `signing` and `signContext` are ignored.
- **The messages above are Kino 0.9.54's**: the technical detail your code and the
  log see is English from that version on and may change, so match on the error's `code`, never on its
  text. Kino 0.9.53 and older word them in Spanish (`La firma por petición solo funciona con video HLS
  (.m3u8)`, "sign no puede usar la red", `El dato "signContext" no es válido`…).
- A signed stream does not use [`alternatives`](contract.md#stream): its failover is the
  `alternateHosts` below.

## Reopening: `resolve(ref, { retry })` { #retry }

If the origin answers 409, or 401/403 twice in a row, Kino calls
`resolve(ref, { retry: { reason, attempt, status } })` again:

- `reason`: `"conflict"` (the access is in use elsewhere: get another one) or `"expired"`;
- `attempt` from 1 to 3;
- `status`, the origin's HTTP status that caused it (401, 403 or 409; absent when Kino did not hear
  one), for your log.

The budget refills once the video has played well for a minute; after the third retry the person sees
the error. `options` is `undefined` on a normal call, and only apiVersion 6 plugins ever get it.

## Other hosts that serve the same stream (`alternateHosts`) { #alternate-hosts }

`alternateHosts`, up to 6 `"host"` or `"host:port"`, no scheme or path. Kino tries the playlist on each,
the one that served last first, for up to 3 rounds, and moves a segment, key or map to another host
when its own fails 3 times. `sign()` always gets the URL of the host being asked, so choose that host's
token from `context`.

```js
return { url: "http://cdn1.example/live/ch.m3u8", signing: "request",
         alternateHosts: ["cdn2.example", "cdn3.example:8080"],
         signContext: JSON.stringify({ "cdn1.example": t1, "cdn2.example": t2, "cdn3.example:8080": t3 }) };
// sign({ url, context }): const tokens = JSON.parse(context); const token = tokens[new URL(url).host];
```

- Each entry meets the same host rule as `url`: a declared host (plain http only on one declared
  `insecureHttp`), or any public host under `liveStreamHosts: "any"`, never a local one.
- An entry that fails it, repeats `url`'s host or another entry, or comes after the sixth is dropped
  (`run.mjs` and `validate.mjs` show it as `[dropped by Kino]`); a value that is not an array of strings
  refuses the stream with `the "alternateHosts" value is not valid` (Kino 0.9.53 and older: `El dato
  "alternateHosts" no es válido`).
- With them, the stream counts as `"expired"` only when **every** host rejected the signature, and as
  `"conflict"` only when the last one answered 409; a host answering 404 or not at all just moves Kino on.
- A host the playlist names that is not one of these is never swapped.
- Ignored without `signing`.

## Chromecast and DLNA { #cast }

A signed stream can be sent to a TV like any other HLS. The TV never signs anything: it pulls the
stream through Kino on the phone, which calls `sign()` for every playlist and segment the TV asks for,
exactly as for its own player (the same 1.5 s limit, the same "three failed signatures stop the
video"). So the phone must stay on the same Wi-Fi as the TV with Kino running for the whole cast.

- If the origin refuses the stream while the TV plays it and the player is still open on the phone,
  Kino calls `resolve(ref, { retry })` again and the TV reloads it from the same point (a live channel
  from its edge).
- Once the person leaves the player, a Chromecast keeps playing until it is stopped or sent something
  else, but a refusal is no longer re-resolved: the TV's playback just ends. Leaving the player stops a
  DLNA TV, as for any title.
- A signed stream with `drm` is never cast. Kino plays one signed stream at a time: opening another one
  on the phone ends the cast of the first.

## Test it from your terminal { #test }

```
node sdk/run.mjs ./plugin.js sign '{"url":"https://cdn.example/seg.ts","kind":"segment","ref":"<ref>","context":"<signContext>"}'
node sdk/run.mjs --retry conflict:1 ./plugin.js resolve '<ref>'      # or conflict:1:409 to pass a status
```

The first runs `sign` in the same restricted lane; the second calls `resolve` with a retry. With
`"telemetry": "verbose"` Kino also reports each playback's signing statistics (p50, p95, max and
timeouts): see [Logs and telemetry](diagnostics.md#playback).


<!-- page: https://kinotvapp.github.io/kino-plugins/en/resolver/ (docs/resolver.en.md) -->

# External resolver apps { #resolver }

Everything else in this guide runs inside Kino's sandbox: a plugin reads a site, a JSON API or your own
server and hands Kino a URL. Some sources cannot be turned into a URL that way. They need a real program on
the device: a download engine, a media pipeline that converts a format the phone cannot decode, a helper that
speaks a protocol the sandbox has no access to. Kino does not contain such programs and does not know how any
of them works. Instead it has a small **open protocol**: a plugin names *what* it found, and an
independently-installed Android app, an **external resolver**, turns it into something Kino can play.

This page is for three readers: the plugin author who wants to use a resolver, the developer who wants to
build one, and anyone who needs to know what to expect. It needs `"apiVersion": 11` (Kino 0.9.66) and the
`externalResolve` capability.

## What it is, and what it is not { #what }

- **It is** one extra hop in the life of a `resolve()`: your plugin answers `{ external: { protocol, ref } }`
  instead of a `url`; Kino hands `protocol` and `ref` to an installed app that says it handles `protocol`; that
  app answers with the same kind of object a plugin answers with (`url`, `headers`, `subtitles`, `mime`... plus
  `media` and `portable`); Kino plays that.
- **It is not** a way to reach another app in general, a plugin API or a back door around the host rules: Kino
  never sends the app anything but `protocol` and `ref`, never widens your plugin's approved hosts because of
  it, and the app never learns which plugin, title or person it is serving beyond what you put in `ref`.
- **It is not part of Kino.** Kino's own code never branches on the value of `protocol`, and there is no
  registry of names: a protocol name is a string a plugin and a resolver agree on by convention
  (`my-protocol` in the examples). Who builds the resolver, how it gets its content and whether you may use it
  for yours is between you and its author.
- **It is not guaranteed to exist.** Nothing says an app is installed ([what to expect](#expect)).

## Who does what { #roles }

| Piece | Does | Never does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Your plugin** | Finds the title, produces an opaque `ref`, answers `{ external: { protocol, ref } }` (and may name the app: `resolver`, or the manifest's `externalResolver`). | See the app, its answer or how it played. |
| **Kino** | Finds the app, asks the person once, binds it, shows live progress with *Cancelar*, validates the answer with the same rules as a plugin's, plays it (and casts it), shows the person a readable error. | Interpret `ref`, widen your hosts, retry a failure the app explained, ask an app for a download, a preload or a background refresh. |
| **The resolver app** | Does the real work, keeps its own server alive while the player reads, answers `onResult` / `onError`, may say why a later request failed. | Run in Kino's sandbox or talk to your plugin. |

## The flow, step by step { #flow }

```
plugin  resolve("title-42")  ->  { external: { protocol: "my-protocol", ref: "<opaque>", resolver?: "com.example.resolver" } }
Kino    finds an app declaring "my-protocol"; first time: asks the person (Permitir / No permitir)
Kino    binds the app's service  ->  IExternalResolver.resolve("my-protocol", "<opaque>", callback)
app     onProgress(40, "Preparando...")  ...  Kino shows "Abriendo con <app>" with a bar and Cancelar
app     onResult(json)  or  onError(code, message)         (exactly one; Kino's own limit is 120 s for the whole call)
Kino    validates json like a plugin answer, unbinds right away, plays the url
player  reads the url while the app keeps serving (a foreground service)
```

1. **The answer.** `external` can be the whole `resolve()` answer (then `url` may be left out) or one entry of a
   Stream's `alternatives`, next to a concrete `{ url }` copy or a lazy `{ ref }` one
   ([labelled and lazy copies](contract.md#lazy-copies)). `protocol` is 1 to 64 characters from `a-z 0-9 . _ -`;
   `ref` is 1 to 2048 characters with no control characters; `resolver` is an Android package name. A plugin
   below `apiVersion` 11, or one that does not declare `externalResolve`, has `external` ignored and fails like an
   answer with no `url`. A malformed `external` is dropped, never half-read.
2. **Finding the app.** An installed app is a candidate when its manifest declares a `<service>` with the action
   `com.arkiv.player.action.RESOLVE_EXTERNAL` and a `<meta-data
   android:name="com.arkiv.player.meta.RESOLVER_PROTOCOLS" android:value="my-protocol,another">` naming
   `protocol`. When `resolver` (or the manifest's `externalResolver.package`) is set, only that app is a
   candidate; if it is not installed, Kino says so, or offers its download ([below](#expect)).
3. **Consent.** The first time, the person is asked, naming your plugin and the app, and told the app is not
   Kino's. The answer is stored per *(plugin, protocol, app)*, applies from then on and can be revoked in
   Ajustes, in the "Fuentes externas" section. With more than one candidate and no `resolver`, the person picks
   ("Elige qué aplicación usar") and the pick is remembered as the same decision; Kino asks again only when it
   becomes ambiguous. A "no" is remembered too: that title then says "No autorizaste resolver este contenido
   con ...". This is the only consent: your plugin's own install sheet does not change for `externalResolve`.
4. **Binding and the call.** Kino binds the service and calls `resolve(protocol, ref, callback)`. One call at a
   time per binding. The app answers with any number of `onProgress(percent, message)` and then exactly one of
   `onResult(json)` / `onError(code, message)`.
5. **Progress.** Kino shows the latest `onProgress` live: `percent` 0 to 100 as a bar (anything else means
   "indeterminate"), `message` as one short line (whitespace collapsed, control characters dropped, cut at 80
   characters; blank shows Kino's own "Buscando..."). The person can press *Cancelar* or leave the player: Kino
   calls `cancel()`, unbinds and ignores anything the app sends afterwards.
6. **The deadline.** Past 120 s Kino calls `cancel()` and reports `timeout`.
7. **The result.** `onResult`'s JSON is validated by the same code that validates a plugin's `resolve()`
   answer. It differs only in hosts ([below](#answer)), in that **DRM is refused** and that a second `external`
   inside it is `bad_response`: one hop, never a chain.
8. **After the answer.** Kino unbinds at once. The app has to keep itself alive (a foreground service) for as
   long as the player reads from the URL. If it has to refuse a later request it says why in a response header
   ([errors](#errors)).

## What a resolver app can do { #can }

Anything that ends in a URL Kino can play, for example:

- **Serve content it fetches as the player reads it.** A helper that downloads while you watch and answers with
  a URL on its own server on the device (the [loopback](#loopback) case).
- **Convert what the device cannot open.** A 10-bit video, an unusual container or an audio codec nobody
  decodes can be answered as an HLS of 8-bit H.264 and AAC, produced on demand, so the player still gets
  picture and sound.
- **Add tracks.** `subtitles` and `audioTracks` in the answer, or, for an HLS, renditions the manifest itself
  lists (`#EXT-X-MEDIA`).
- **Describe the file.** [`media`](#media) says what the file holds, so Kino can show it and use it as a hint.
- **Offer a universal copy for TVs.** [`portable`](#portable).
- **Explain failures** in a sentence the person reads, before the answer (`onError`) and after it
  (`X-Resolver-Error`).

Things it cannot do: change your plugin's approved hosts, ask the person for anything through Kino, reach other
plugins, return DRM, or be asked outside a person pressing play.

## The answer { #answer }

`onResult` carries the same JSON shape as [a plugin's `resolve()` answer](contract.md#stream):

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `url` | The video. Required. See *Hosts* below. |
| `mime`, `headers`, `subtitles`, `audioTracks`, `durationMs`, `expiresInSeconds` | As for a plugin; `subtitles` and audio track URLs are checked like `url`. |
| `media` | Optional, advisory: what the file holds ([below](#media)). |
| `portable` | Optional: a universal HLS copy of the same video ([below](#portable)). |
| `drm`, `external` | Refused (`bad_response`). |

**Hosts.** The `url` came from the app, not from your plugin, so your declared hosts do not apply: any public
host is accepted, over `https` or `http`, for the video, its subtitles and audio tracks and everything its
manifest names while it plays; never an address on the home network, a local name or a private IP. That
allowance belongs to this one playback and is never added to your plugin's approved hosts; Kino never asks the
person to widen them for it.

### The loopback origin { #loopback }

An app that has the content locally may answer with the URL of its own server on the device:
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/...`, plain http, host exactly `127.0.0.1`, port 1024 or higher, no credentials. That
one origin, taken from this very answer, is accepted for that playback (never `localhost`, another address,
IPv6, https on loopback or a low port; a redirect from elsewhere into it is refused). Put an unguessable token
in the path: any app on the device can reach loopback. The server should answer `GET` and `HEAD` with `Range`
(a player seeks with it).

### `media` { #media }

Optional and advisory, and a plugin's own `resolve()` answer may carry the same object (see
[The `Stream` rules](contract.md#stream)). Every field is optional and cleaned: one-line text cut at 120
characters (`codec`/`container` 40, `language` 20), numbers clamped, at most 16 tracks and 4 `notes`; an object
with nothing usable left is dropped, never an error.

```json
"media": {
  "title": "Movie.mkv", "sizeBytes": 1234567890, "container": "matroska,webm",
  "video": { "codec": "h264", "profile": "High 10", "width": 1920, "height": 1080, "fps": 23.976, "bitDepth": 10, "hdr": false },
  "audio": [ { "codec": "eac3", "channels": 6, "language": "eng", "title": "Original", "default": true } ],
  "subtitles": [ { "codec": "subrip", "language": "eng", "title": "", "text": true } ],
  "converted": true, "notes": ["no decoder for H.264 High 10 on this device"]
}
```

The tracks are the *file's*, whether or not the app converted them for the player (`converted`). Kino logs a
summary (codecs and counts, never a title or a note), carries `media` to the player and may use it as a hint
when it decides how to cast. It never trusts it for anything that could harm the person. Showing it to the
person is not built yet.

### `portable` { #portable }

`{ "url": "...", "mime": "application/x-mpegURL" }`: **a universal version of the same video**, which the app
can make on demand and any TV receiver plays: HLS, H.264 8-bit up to 1080p, stereo AAC, its audio tracks and
text subtitles as HLS renditions. It must cost nothing until something reads it. It is checked like `url`; a
non-HLS `mime`, or a URL that fails the checks, drops the `portable` and keeps the rest of the answer. It is
ignored next to DRM or request signing. The phone's own player never uses it.

## Errors the person reads { #errors }

| When | What the app sends | What the person sees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before the answer | `onError(code, message)`, `code` one of `unavailable`, `timeout`, `cancelled`, `unsupported`, `bad_response`, `other` (anything else is read as `other`) | "No se pudo resolver este contenido (`code`): `message`." The message is the app's own sentence, cleaned to one line of at most 120 characters and shown as the app's words, so keep it short and plain. |
| After the answer, when its server cannot serve a request | An HTTP 4xx/5xx with the header `X-Resolver-Error: <code>; <message>` (ASCII, at most 120 characters) | The player's error line "La aplicación que ofrece este video dijo: `message`", and Kino does not retry it. Only this origin's responses are read this way. |
| Kino's own failures | Nothing | Only the code: "No se pudo resolver este contenido (`unavailable`)" when the app cannot be bound, `timeout` past 120 s, `bad_response` for a JSON that fails the checks. Their English detail goes to the log, never the screen. |
| No app, a denial, the picked app gone | Nothing | "Este contenido necesita una aplicación externa que no tienes instalada.", "No autorizaste resolver este contenido con ...", "La aplicación que elegiste ya no está instalada." |

## Casting a resolver's title { #cast }

A TV can never reach `127.0.0.1`, so a title from a resolver is never handed to a TV by its own URL. Kino serves
it through its own cast proxy on the phone, which reads the resolver's origin and gives the TV a token URL on
the local network ([Sending to the TV](what-people-see.md#cast)). That means:

- the app's server must answer `GET` and `HEAD` with `Range`; every read through the proxy reaches it as an
  ordinary request (so it keeps an idle timer alive);
- an HLS answer is rewritten for the receiver, renditions included (`#EXT-X-MEDIA` audio and WebVTT
  subtitles), and a progressive file goes the way any plugin file does (the proxy, or the phone's remux when
  the cast method asks for it);
- when the title's own route would need a conversion, or `media` says the video is not something a receiver
  takes as it is (not H.264, deeper than 8 bits, above 1080p, HDR, a DTS or TrueHD main audio) and the stream
  is not already a conversion, Kino casts the app's **`portable`** copy instead, when it offered one. The phone
  keeps playing the title itself;
- a title with DRM, request signing, a live channel or music never uses `portable`.

This is covered by Kino's tests with a fake resolver and was tried on one real Chromecast (a TV's built-in one): a direct H.264
file, a converted HLS with audio and subtitle renditions (seeking from the phone works) and a `portable` copy of an HEVC file all play.
**DLNA** was tried on one real LG webOS TV, which lists no HLS in its formats yet plays it: Kino sends it the HLS playlist as it is, and both a converted HLS with audio and subtitle renditions and a muxed `portable` copy reached playing, with the real duration and a position that advances (pause and resume from the phone work). The "continuous MPEG-TS" route Kino uses for a TV that cannot play HLS does **not** play on that TV, so keep an HLS answer for it. Not tried: sending a plain progressive file from the first byte (one attempt stalled at the TV), seeking from the TV, other renderers, and confirming the picture on the screen. Also untried: an app that survives the phone's
screen turning off.

## What to expect { #expect }

- **Maybe no app is installed.** Your plugin is not told. The person reads "Este contenido necesita una
  aplicación externa que no tienes instalada." (or, when your manifest names the app with an `apk`, is offered
  to download it). Say in your description that your plugin needs it, and give it a real fallback when you can:
  a `url` your own code can produce, with `external` kept to one of several `alternatives`.
- **Only while the person plays.** Never for a preload, a background refresh or a download: an
  externally-resolved title says it can only be played ("Este contenido lo abre una aplicación externa: solo se
  puede reproducir.").
- **120 seconds** for the whole call, one hop only, DRM never.
- **Every app is the person's choice, not yours.** They can say no, pick another, or revoke later.
- **You never learn which app handled it, or how.** Either the stream plays, or `resolve` fails like any other
  failure.
- **Offering the download.** When your manifest's [`externalResolver`](manifest.md#external-resolver) has an
  `apk` (`url` on a GitHub release asset or an archive.org file, `sha256`, optional `label`) and the app is missing, Kino shows a
  sheet: it can download it from GitHub, checks the file has exactly that `sha256` (otherwise it is deleted and
  nothing is offered) and hands it to Android's installer, which asks the person as for any app. Kino does not
  check who signed it and has not reviewed it; the sheet says so.
- **Other ways to get the app.** `externalResolver` may also say `"fdroid": true` (the same `package` is listed in F-Droid:
  Kino opens the F-Droid client for exactly that package, or its page on f-droid.org, or says what to search for) and/or
  `"downloader": { "code": "..." }` (3 to 10 digits: a code of the Downloader app that sideloads on a TV; Kino only **shows** it,
  with a button to open Downloader when it is installed, and installs nothing itself on that path). All three are optional and
  independent, Kino offers only what is declared for exactly that `package`, and the sheet leads with the buttons on a phone and
  with the code on a TV. Be honest with your users: the official F-Droid client has no real Android TV support (it does not appear
  in the TV's launcher and some screens cannot be reached with a remote), so for a TV the Downloader code or the `apk` is the
  practical route. Kino has not verified a particular F-Droid client build against this link on a real device.
- **The app for a computer.** If your resolver also runs on a computer, `externalResolver` may carry
  `"desktop": { "windows": { "url": "...", "sha256": "..." }, "linux": { ... }, "macos": { ... } }`: each a GitHub release
  asset (a zip, see "Desktop transport" in the resolver protocol) and the `sha256` its bytes must have. Kino on a computer
  reads only the entry for its own system and never your `apk`; Kino on Android never reads `desktop`. Same rules as the
  `apk`: Kino downloads it from GitHub, checks the `sha256` (otherwise it is deleted and nothing is installed) and has not
  reviewed what is in it. A system you leave out simply has no app offered.

## Using a resolver from your plugin { #use }

1. **Manifest:** `"apiVersion": 11`, `"externalResolve"` in `capabilities` and, to name the app,
   `externalResolver`:

   ```json
   {
     "apiVersion": 11,
     "capabilities": ["search", "home", "resolve", "externalResolve"],
     "externalResolver": {
       "package": "com.example.resolver",
       "apk": { "url": "https://github.com/example/resolver/releases/download/v1.0.0/resolver.apk", "sha256": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef", "label": "My Resolver" }
     }
   }
   ```

   `hosts` is still the set of sites *your* code reaches (your catalog), not what the resolver reaches. A
   manifest must name at least one, even if the plugin does no networking.
2. **`resolve(ref)`** answers the hand-off:

   ```js
   export async function resolve(ref) {
     const entry = CATALOG[ref];
     if (!entry) throw kino.error("not_found", "ya no está");
     return { external: { protocol: "my-protocol", ref: entry.reference } };   // add resolver: "com.example.resolver" to force that app
   }
   ```

3. **Several copies** (qualities, releases): as `alternatives`, each `{ label, ref }` lazy copy resolved by your
   own `resolve` and answering `external` again, or an entry `{ external, label }` directly ([labelled and lazy
   copies](contract.md#lazy-copies)). The person moves to the next copy when one fails.
4. **Test offline** with the kit: `node sdk/run.mjs . resolve <ref>` applies Kino's output rules, so you see
   whether your `external` survives (it is ignored without `apiVersion` 11 and the capability) and how `media`
   and `portable` come out. The kit cannot run a resolver app: to see the whole hand-off you need the app
   installed on a device ([Test it locally](test-locally.md)).

## Building a resolver { #build }

The other side is an Android app with one bound service. The contract is small:

```aidl
package com.arkiv.player.resolver.contract;

interface IExternalResolver {
    /** protocol: 1..64 chars [a-z0-9._-]+. ref: 1..2048 chars, opaque. At most one resolve() in flight per binding. */
    oneway void resolve(String protocol, String ref, IExternalResolverCallback callback);
    /** Best effort: whatever resolve() is running ends with onError("cancelled", ...). */
    oneway void cancel();
}

interface IExternalResolverCallback {
    /** Zero or more times. percent: -1 = indeterminate, else 0..100. message: shown verbatim, trusted only as display text. */
    oneway void onProgress(int percent, String message);
    /** Exactly one of onResult/onError ends a resolve() call. */
    oneway void onResult(String resultJson);
    /** code: one of "unavailable","timeout","cancelled","unsupported","bad_response","other". */
    oneway void onError(String code, String message);
}
```

Declare the service so Kino finds it:

```xml
<service android:name=".MyResolverService" android:exported="true" android:foregroundServiceType="dataSync">
  <intent-filter><action android:name="com.arkiv.player.action.RESOLVE_EXTERNAL" /></intent-filter>
  <meta-data android:name="com.arkiv.player.meta.RESOLVER_PROTOCOLS" android:value="my-protocol" />
</service>
```

In short: implement `resolve(protocol, ref, callback)` off the binder thread (answer fast with progress, end with
exactly one `onResult` or `onError`), keep your server alive in a foreground service while the player reads,
answer `Range` and `HEAD`, put an unguessable token in your URLs, answer an unservable request with an HTTP
error and a readable `X-Resolver-Error: <code>; <message>`, and return the same URL when the same content is
resolved again (a player that still holds the old URL must not be left on a dead one). The protocol is open:
nothing checks who signed your app, and anyone may implement it. The full wire-level contract, with every limit,
is `resolver-contract/PROTOCOL.md` in Kino's source repository.

## Security model { #security }

- The protocol is **open**: nothing checks who signed the other app, and anyone may implement it. The person's
  per-app consent, and Android's own install prompt, are the trust decisions.
- Kino sends the app only `protocol` and `ref`, and only after consent.
- The app's text reaches the screen only as one cleaned, bounded line; its codes are whitelisted.
- Its URLs pass the plugin-answer checks; the only local address ever accepted is the one loopback origin of
  that answer, for that playback, for the first request (never as a redirect target).
- DRM and chains are refused; a failure is never retried once the app has explained it.

## FAQ { #faq }

**Can my plugin check that a resolver is installed?** No. Kino tells the person; your plugin is not told. Ship
a fallback.

**Does the resolver see my plugin's settings or secrets?** No. It receives `protocol` and `ref`, nothing else.

**Can one `ref` serve several apps?** Only by convention: `ref` is yours and the protocol name is a string you
share with whoever builds the app. Name the app in `externalResolver` when only one will do.

**Why is the `url` allowed to be `http://127.0.0.1:...`?** Because an app that serves the content from the
device has to; it is accepted for that one answer, with an unguessable path token in it, and for nothing else.

**Will it cast?** Through Kino's proxy: Chromecast and DLNA yes for an HLS answer (each tried on one real receiver)
([above](#cast)).

**Where do I see what `media` said?** In Kino's log, as a one-line summary. A screen for it is not built yet.


<!-- page: https://kinotvapp.github.io/kino-plugins/en/protocol/ (docs/protocol.en.md) -->

# The plugin protocol: plugins that use each other { #protocol }

!!! note "Available from Kino 0.9.81"
    The plugin protocol is `apiVersion` 20 and ships with Kino 0.9.81. Every older Kino refuses a manifest with
    `"apiVersion": 20` («Este plugin necesita una versión más nueva de Kino»), but a plugin that stays on a lower
    `apiVersion` can still open its doors through [`enhancements["20"]`](#versions), which an older Kino ignores. Every number
    on this page is in `contract.json`, section `protocol` ([Reference](reference/index.md)).

A Kino plugin can **build on another plugin**. One plugin, the **provider**, opens named **doors** in its manifest: a few
calls (question and answer) and streams (news it publishes every so often), each with the shape of what it receives and what
it returns. Another plugin, the **consumer**, lists the doors it uses and asks them with
`await kino.plugins.call(alias, call, arg)`. **Kino is the only middleman**: the two plugins never see each other, never
share memory and never call each other directly. Kino finds the provider, checks every request and every answer against the
types the provider declared, limits the rate and reports a clear error code when something is missing.

Why it exists: so that work done once can be reused by everyone. A plugin that knows how to talk to a service (TMDB, a
music catalog, a sports feed) can offer that knowledge as a door, and other plugins (a game, a widget, a recommendations
screen) use it without copying its code, its hosts or its keys.

The first real pair, used as the example all along this page:

| Plugin | Role | Repository |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **TMDB** | Provider: opens the `movies` door (find a movie by id, a random one, search, and a `trending` stream) | [kinotvapp/kino-plugin-tmdb](https://github.com/kinotvapp/kino-plugin-tmdb) (TMDB 1.3.0 and later) |
| **Cine Trivia** | Consumer: a five-question movie trivia that takes every movie from TMDB's door | [kinotvapp/kino-plugin-cine-trivia](https://github.com/kinotvapp/kino-plugin-cine-trivia) |

!!! info "TMDB 1.3.0 and later, Kino 0.9.81 or newer"
    The `movies` door arrives in TMDB 1.3.0 and later. It sits in `enhancements["20"]`, so TMDB keeps its `apiVersion` and
    keeps installing on older Kinos, but **only Kino 0.9.81 or newer opens the door**: on an older Kino, TMDB is the
    same catalog plugin as always and Cine Trivia (which declares `apiVersion` 20) does not install.

## In one minute { #summary }

- **Provider:** declares `provides` in `kino-plugin.json` and exports one function per call, `proto_<door>_<call>(arg)`, and
  one per stream, `proto_<door>_<stream>(cursor)`.
- **Consumer:** declares `consumes` (an alias, the provider's `repo`, the `door`, the calls and streams it uses) and also
  `recommends` the provider, so it can offer to install it.
- **The call:** `const movie = await kino.plugins.call("tmdb", "random", { fromYear: 1990 })`. It resolves to the provider's
  answer, already checked against the declared type, or rejects with an `Error` whose `code` is one of seven.
- **A stream:** the consumer's screen sets `state.protocol.<alias>.<stream> = true`; Kino polls the provider and delivers the
  new items to `screenEvent` as the event `protocol`.
- **Nothing installs on its own.** While the provider is missing, the consumer draws only an install screen with a
  [`go.installPlugin`](screen-forms.md#go-install-plugin) button. Kino opens its normal install sheet; the person decides.
- **Kino checks everything:** requests strictly, answers loosely (undeclared fields are dropped), 64 KB each way, 10 s per
  call, 30 calls in any 10 s per door. 18+ content never crosses into a plugin that is not 18+, sealed secrets never cross at
  all.
- **Sharing to Kino Social** is a consumer of this protocol: Kino Social's `wall` door and its `share` call. See
  [Sharing](share.md).

## The mental model { #model }

Kino sits in the middle of every exchange. Neither plugin knows where the other one lives; they only know a door name and the
types written in the provider's manifest.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Cine Trivia (consumer)
    participant K as Kino
    participant T as TMDB (provider)
    C->>K: kino.plugins.call("tmdb", "random", { fromYear: 1990 })
    Note over K: alias in consumes? call listed?<br/>provider installed and on? 18+ rule?<br/>under 30 calls / 10 s for this door?
    Note over K: argument checked against "in" (strict)
    K->>T: proto_movies_random({ fromYear: 1990 })
    T-->>K: { id, title, year, director, internalScore }
    Note over K: answer checked against "out" (loose):<br/>internalScore dropped, no sealed secret
    K-->>C: { id, title, year, director }
```

| Who | Does | Never does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The provider** | Declares its doors and their types; answers each call with JSON; decides in code what to share | Learns which plugin asked before Kino 0.9.84 (from then on [`ctx.caller`](share.md#ctx-caller) says it); reaches the consumer; sends a type it did not declare (Kino drops it) |
| **The consumer** | Declares what it uses; calls with an argument that matches `in`; handles the error codes; invites the person to install the provider | Calls a door it did not list; installs anything; reads the provider's storage, settings or secrets |
| **Kino** | Finds the provider by repository, validates both ways, limits the rate and the time, runs streams while a screen is open, shows the consent line | Stores anything about the exchange (nothing new is synced); asks the person on every call |
| **The person** | Sees "Usa datos de TMDB (Movie records from TMDB)" on the consumer's install sheet; installs the provider with their own tap | Gets a plugin installed without tapping Instalar |

A door is not a capability. A provider keeps the capabilities of the kind of plugin it is (TMDB is still a catalog with
`search`, `home`, `meta`...), and a consumer keeps its own (Cine Trivia is a `screen` plugin). `provides` and `consumes` are
two extra manifest blocks next to them.

## A complete example: TMDB and Cine Trivia { #example }

### The provider: TMDB opens the `movies` door { #example-provider }

TMDB is an existing catalog plugin on `apiVersion` 7. To open its door **without raising its `apiVersion`** (so it keeps
installing on every Kino it already supports) it puts `provides` inside `enhancements["20"]`. This is the part of
`kino-plugin.json` that TMDB 1.3.0 adds (the rest of the manifest, its capabilities and settings, is unchanged):

```json
{
  "id": "tmdb",
  "name": "TMDB",
  "version": "1.3.0",
  "apiVersion": 7,
  "entry": "plugin.js",
  "hosts": ["image.tmdb.org"],
  "capabilities": ["search", "home", "browse", "episodes", "resolve", "meta"],
  "enhancements": {
    "20": {
      "provides": {
        "movies": {
          "summary": "Movie records from TMDB",
          "calls": {
            "byId":   { "in": { "id": "number" }, "out": "Movie" },
            "random": { "in": { "fromYear": "number?", "toYear": "number?" }, "out": "Movie" },
            "search": { "in": { "q": "string" }, "out": "Movie[]" }
          },
          "streams": {
            "trending": { "out": "Movie", "everySeconds": 60 }
          },
          "types": {
            "Movie": { "id": "number", "title": "string", "year": "number", "director": "string?", "overview": "string?", "posterUrl": "string?" }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Read it as the door's documentation: `byId` takes `{ id }` and answers one `Movie`; `random` takes an optional year range and
answers one `Movie`; `search` takes `{ q }` and answers a list of `Movie`; `trending` is a stream of `Movie`, polled at most
once a minute. A `Movie` always has `id`, `title` and `year`, and may have `director`, `overview` and `posterUrl`.

Each call and stream is one export of the entry file, named `proto_<door>_<name>`. TMDB answers through Kino's own
[`kino.tmdb`](kino-api.md#tmdb) service, so it needs no host and no key of its own for this:

```js
// The "movies" door. Kino checks every argument against "in" before calling, and every answer against "out" after.
export async function proto_movies_byId(arg) {
  return movieById(arg && arg.id);                 // one kino.tmdb request (credits included, for the director)
}

export async function proto_movies_random(arg) {
  const { fromYear, toYear } = arg || {};          // both optional: Kino passes {} when the consumer sends nothing
  const params = { include_adult: false, sort_by: "popularity.desc", "vote_count.gte": 100 };
  if (Number.isInteger(fromYear)) params["primary_release_date.gte"] = `${fromYear}-01-01`;
  if (Number.isInteger(toYear)) params["primary_release_date.lte"] = `${toYear}-12-31`;
  const pool = await discoverPool({ ...params, page: 1 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 10) });
  if (!pool.length) throw new Error("not_found");  // a throw reaches the consumer as provider_failed
  return movieById(pool[Math.floor(Math.random() * pool.length)].id);
}

export async function proto_movies_search(arg) {
  const q = String(arg.q).trim().slice(0, 200);
  return q ? moviesOf(await kino.tmdb("/search/movie", { query: q, include_adult: false })) : [];
}

// A stream: the argument is the cursor this function returned last time (null the first time).
export async function proto_movies_trending(cursor) {
  const seen = Array.isArray(cursor) ? cursor : [];
  const fresh = moviesOf(await kino.tmdb("/trending/movie/week", {})).filter((m) => !seen.includes(m.id));
  return { items: fresh, cursor: seen.concat(fresh.map((m) => m.id)).slice(-200) };
}
```

`movieById`, `discoverPool` and `moviesOf` are TMDB's own helpers: they turn TMDB's rows into the declared `Movie`
(`{ id, title, year, director?, overview?, posterUrl? }`) and leave adult rows out. The complete code is in the TMDB
repository.

### The consumer: Cine Trivia { #example-consumer }

Cine Trivia is useless without TMDB, so it declares `apiVersion` 20 directly. Its manifest:

```json
{
  "id": "cine-trivia",
  "name": "Cine Trivia",
  "version": "1.0.1",
  "apiVersion": 20,
  "entry": "plugin.js",
  "description": "Cinco preguntas de cine, quince segundos cada una: las películas llegan del plugin TMDB",
  "hosts": [],
  "capabilities": ["screen"],
  "screen": { "label": "Cine Trivia", "labelEn": "Cine Trivia", "icon": "movie", "menuOpens": "screen" },
  "recommends": ["kinotvapp/kino-plugin-tmdb"],
  "consumes": {
    "tmdb": {
      "repo": "kinotvapp/kino-plugin-tmdb",
      "door": "movies",
      "calls": ["random", "byId"],
      "streams": ["trending"]
    }
  }
}
```

- `consumes.tmdb`: `tmdb` is a **local alias**, the first argument of `kino.plugins.call`. `repo` is the provider's GitHub
  repository, `door` the door's name, `calls` and `streams` exactly the names Cine Trivia uses (it never calls `search`, so it
  does not list it).
- `recommends` names the same repository, so `screen` and `screenEvent` receive `installed["kinotvapp/kino-plugin-tmdb"]`
  (see [the install gate](#install-gate)).
- `hosts` is `[]`: Cine Trivia is a [screen-only consumer](#consumer-hosts). The movie data does not come from the network
  (it comes through Kino from the provider), and the posters it draws (TMDB's `posterUrl`) are public images, which need no
  host declaration.

### The install gate { #install-gate }

Kino never installs anything on its own. Until TMDB is installed, Cine Trivia shows **only** an install screen with one
button. The button's `go` is [`installPlugin`](screen-forms.md#go-install-plugin): Kino opens its normal install sheet over
the screen, and the person taps Instalar (or Cancelar).

```js
const TMDB_REPO = "kinotvapp/kino-plugin-tmdb";
const gateOpen = (installed) => !!installed && installed[TMDB_REPO] === true;

export async function screen({ state = {}, installed } = {}) {
  if (!gateOpen(installed)) return installView();        // nothing else is drawn or interactive
  return gameView(state);
}

function installView() {
  return {
    type: "Column", padding: 24, gap: 16, crossAxisAlignment: "center", children: [
      { type: "Text", text: "Cine Trivia", textEn: "Cine Trivia", style: "h1", textAlign: "center" },
      { type: "Text", text: "Para jugar necesitas el plugin TMDB: de ahí salen las películas de cada pregunta.",
        textEn: "To play you need the TMDB plugin: every question's movies come from it.", textAlign: "center" },
      { type: "ElevatedButton", key: "install", labelText: "Instalar TMDB", labelTextEn: "Install TMDB", autofocus: true,
        onPressed: { go: { installPlugin: { repo: TMDB_REPO } } } },
    ],
  };
}

export async function screenEvent({ name, installed } = {}) {
  if (!gateOpen(installed)) return null;                  // no event does anything until TMDB is there
  // ... the game
}
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[The person opens Cine Trivia] --> B{"installed[TMDB]?"}
    B -- false --> C[Install screen:<br/>one button]
    C -- "go.installPlugin" --> D[Kino's install sheet<br/>for TMDB]
    D -- Instalar --> E[installed flips to true;<br/>Kino calls screen again]
    D -- Cancelar --> C
    B -- true --> F[The game]
    E --> F
```

When the person installs TMDB, `installed` changes and Kino calls `screen` again while the screen is open: the game appears in
place, without reopening the plugin. From then on it loads straight away. If the person removes TMDB later, Cine Trivia is
not touched: the gate simply shows the install screen again, and any call that was in flight answers `provider_missing`.

**What `installed` says, exactly.** `installed["<owner/name>"]` is `true` while a plugin installed from that repository is on
the device, **even when the person switched it off or it still needs its settings**; it is `false` only when no plugin from
that repository is installed (never installed, or removed). So the gate alone is not enough: with `installed` `true` a call can
still answer `provider_missing` (the provider is off, needs setup, or is 18+ while your plugin is not). Keep that code in your
state and draw a sentence for it, such as «TMDB está apagado o le falta configurarse: revísalo en Plugins», with a retry
button, not the install button (a `go.installPlugin` for a plugin that is already installed only shows Kino's toast «Ese
plugin ya está instalado»). `recommends` does nothing else: Kino shows the person no list or badge for it, it only fills
`installed` (an older Kino ignores the field).

### Asking a door { #calling }

Each round asks TMDB for one random movie of a random era. Kino keeps a screen's state, so the handler calls, answers with
new `state` and keeps nothing alive between events:

```js
async function round(game) {
  try {
    const movie = await kino.plugins.call("tmdb", "random", eraArg(Math.random));   // e.g. { fromYear: 1990, toYear: 1999 }
    const q = buildQuestion(movie);                                                  // movie is a checked Movie
    return { state: { game: { ...game, phase: "question", q, error: null } }, focus: "opt0" };
  } catch (e) {
    const code = e && typeof e.code === "string" ? e.code : "provider_failed";
    return { state: { game: { ...game, phase: "error", error: code } }, focus: "retry" };   // the view offers "Reintentar"
  }
}
```

The answer is exactly the declared `Movie`: if TMDB had added a field the door does not declare, Kino would have dropped it
before Cine Trivia saw it. If TMDB had answered without `title`, the call would reject with `bad_output` instead.

### Live news with a stream { #stream-example }

Cine Trivia has a "Tendencias en vivo" switch. Turning it on sets a state flag; Kino then polls TMDB's `trending` stream while
the screen is open and delivers the new movies as the event `protocol`:

```js
export async function screenEvent({ name, arg, value, state = {}, installed } = {}) {
  if (!gateOpen(installed)) return null;
  switch (name) {
    case "trending":                                  // the Switch's onChanged
      return { state: { protocol: { tmdb: { trending: value === true } }, trendingTitle: null } };
    case "protocol": {                                // arg: { alias: "tmdb", stream: "trending", items: [Movie, ...] }
      if (arg.alias !== "tmdb" || arg.stream !== "trending") return null;
      const movie = arg.items.find((m) => typeof m.title === "string" && m.title.trim());
      return movie ? { state: { trendingTitle: movie.title.slice(0, 120) } } : null;
    }
    // ...
  }
}
```

### What happens on one call, step by step { #steps }

1. Cine Trivia's `screenEvent` runs `kino.plugins.call("tmdb", "random", { fromYear: 1990 })`.
2. Kino looks up the alias `tmdb` in Cine Trivia's `consumes` and checks that `random` is listed there (else `not_declared`).
3. Kino finds the installed plugin whose repository is `kinotvapp/kino-plugin-tmdb` (a fork does not count). If there is none,
   or it is off, or it needs setup, or it is 18+ and Cine Trivia is not, the call is `provider_missing`.
4. Kino checks that TMDB's door `movies` still declares `random` (else `not_declared`) and that Cine Trivia has made fewer than
   30 calls to that door in the last 10 s (else `rate_limited`).
5. Kino checks the argument against `random`'s `in`, strictly (else `bad_input`).
6. Kino calls TMDB's export `proto_movies_random` as a background call, for at most 10 s (else `timeout`; a throw or a missing
   export is `provider_failed`).
7. Kino checks the answer against `random`'s `out`, loosely: it drops undeclared fields, refuses a missing or mistyped
   required field, anything over 64 KB, and any answer that holds one of TMDB's sealed secrets (all `bad_output`).
8. The promise in Cine Trivia resolves to the checked `Movie`.

## The provider in detail { #provider }

### The `provides` block { #provides }

`provides` maps a door name to its declaration. A plugin opens **at most 4 doors**.

| Field of a door | What it is | Rules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `summary` | One sentence for the person: it appears in the consumer's consent line, after your plugin's name | Optional, at most 120 characters. One text for both languages (there is no `summaryEn`): keep it short and plain |
| `calls` | `{ "<call>": { "in"?, "out" } }`, question and answer | At most 16. `out` is required; `in` may be left out for a call with no argument |
| `streams` | `{ "<stream>": { "out", "everySeconds"? } }`, subscriptions | At most 8. `out` is the type of **one item**; `everySeconds` is clamped between 30 and 86,400 (60 when omitted) |
| `types` | `{ "<Type>": { "<field>": "<type>" } }`, named object types | Names start with a capital letter (`^[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]{0,31}$`) and are local to the door |

Door, call, stream (and, on the consumer side, alias) names are letters and digits starting with a letter, at most 32
(`^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]{0,31}$`). A call and a stream of the same door cannot share a name. A malformed block refuses the
whole manifest with a message that names the door and the field (for example `door "movies": call "random" needs an "out"`);
inside `enhancements["20"]` it drops only that block instead.

### The exports { #exports }

| Declared | Export | Receives | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a call `random` of the door `movies` | `proto_movies_random` | the consumer's argument, already checked against `in` (`{}` when the consumer sent none and every field of `in` is optional) | JSON that matches `out` (a value or a promise of one) |
| a stream `trending` of the door `movies` | `proto_movies_trending` | the `cursor` you returned last time, `null` the first time | `{ items: [...], cursor }`: `items` are new since that cursor, each one an `out`; `cursor` is any small JSON you want back next time: it travels inside this answer, at most 64 KB together with the items |

- **Who calls (`ctx`, Kino 0.9.84).** Every `proto_` export also gets a second argument, `ctx`, that Kino fills in and the
  consumer can neither send nor change: `ctx.caller` is `{ id, repo, name, adult }` of the calling plugin. Use it to answer
  differently per caller; a provider that declares only `(arg)` keeps working, and an older Kino sends no `ctx`. Cut the
  `@ref` off `repo` before using it in a `go.plugin`. [`ctx.caller`](share.md#ctx-caller).
- **Throw to fail.** A thrown error reaches the consumer as `provider_failed` (the message is not passed on, so put nothing
  private in it). A missing export is also `provider_failed`.
- **You decide what to share.** The export is ordinary code: answer what you want to give out and nothing more. Kino adds a
  safety net (it drops undeclared fields and refuses sealed secrets), but the first filter is yours.
- **It runs as a background call.** A provider that takes more than 10 s fails that call with `timeout`, but Kino does not mark
  it "No responde" for it, and a provider's failure never touches the consumer's other work or other plugins.
