```json
  "sync": { "mode": "poll", "keySecret": "token", "provision": ["token"] }
}
```

`keySecret` names the setting the sync key comes from; `provision` lists what "Enviar configuración"
hands to a second device (it must include `keySecret`); `"devices": ["phone"]` draws the token field on
the phone only, because a TV receives it.

**2. The code** (`plugin.js`):

```js
const API = "https://sync.example.com";
const auth = () => ({ Authorization: "Bearer " + kino.config.get("token") });

// The stored copy and its version, or null when nothing is stored yet.
export async function syncPull() {
  const r = await kino.fetch(API + "/blob", { headers: auth() });
  if (r.status === 404) return null;
  if (r.status === 401) throw kino.error("auth_required", "token refused");
  if (!r.ok) throw kino.error("unavailable", "pull " + r.status);
  const { blob, version } = r.json();
  return { blob, version };
}

// Stores the copy only if the server still holds expectedVersion; a 409 means another device was faster.
export async function syncPush({ blob, expectedVersion }) {
  const r = await kino.fetch(API + "/blob", {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: { ...auth(), "If-Match": expectedVersion ?? "" },
    body: { json: { blob } },
  });
  if (r.status === 409) throw kino.error("conflict", "the stored copy changed");
  if (r.status === 401) throw kino.error("auth_required", "token refused");
  if (!r.ok) throw kino.error("unavailable", "push " + r.status);
  return { version: r.json().version };
}
```

**3. Test it with the kit**: `node sdk/validate.mjs .` checks the manifest and the `sync` block as Kino
does (these two files pass it) and shows the red consent line; then test the two exports against a
local imitation of your service with `node --test` ([test it locally](#test)).

**4. Publish it**: a public GitHub repository with the files at its root and the `kino-plugin` topic
([publish](publish.md)); people install it by typing `owner/repo`. Sign it if you want people to know
every update is yours, and ask to be [listed](listed.md) if you want it in Kino's recommended plugins.

The rest of this page is the reference. Three complete providers, with guides anyone can follow, are
public repositories: [kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-gram](https://github.com/kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-gram),
[kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-server](https://github.com/kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-server) and
[kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-gram-account](https://github.com/kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-gram-account)
([the three examples](#examples)); the kit is
[kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sdk](https://github.com/kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sdk).

## Is it the right tool? { #when }

- **Yes**, if your plugin can store one file of up to 4 MiB somewhere the person controls and read it
  back later, with an `https` API on a public host.
- **No**, for anything else: a provider cannot see or change what Kino syncs, cannot sync only some
  tables, and does not replace pairing (remote control and sending to the TV stay on the local
  network).
- The person picks **one** provider, or none: in **Ajustes de todos los perfiles ▸ Sincronización ▸
  Proveedor** ("Settings for all profiles ▸ Sync ▸ Provider") the list has **Red local** and every
  installed provider, each with a switch. Turning one on turns the previous one off (Kino asks first:
  "¿Sincronizar con <name>?", with "Combinar con este aparato"); turning the active one off leaves
  sync off. The choice belongs to that device and never syncs: each device turns its provider on
  itself, with the settings it typed or [received](#provisioning). Each provider is drawn as its own
  card there, with its status, its buttons and its "Sincronizar cada" (the red consent line is on the
  install sheet and in the switch-on confirmation, not on the card). The buttons follow the provider's
  state: **"Configurar"** ("Set up") opens your settings form, and on a device that does not hold your
  `provision` values yet the card leads with "Recibir configuración" ([details](#provisioning)).
- Your plugin's own page in Ajustes (phone and TV) starts with Kino's button **"Sincronización ▸
  Proveedor"**, which opens that list (on the TV with your provider's card focused); you declare nothing
  for it. Mark the setup the TV cannot do with [`devices`](settings-form.md#devices) so the TV shows only
  what it needs.

## Who sees what { #who-sees-what }

Kino compresses the snapshot and encrypts it as a whole (AES-256-GCM) before calling your plugin. The
blob your code receives is ciphertext, and Kino never hands your code the key. The key, though, always
comes from your plugin's own settings:

- **Every provider declares [`sync.keySecret`](#sync-block)**, the `key` of one of its `password`
  settings. A manifest with `syncProvider` and no `keySecret` is refused (`The "syncProvider" capability
  needs a "sync" field whose "keySecret" is the key of one of the plugin's own "password" settings`), in
  the app and in the kit. Even when Kino makes that value itself ([`generateKey`](#generate-key)), the key
  comes from that setting.
- **Kino derives the sync key** on each device from that setting's value (HKDF-SHA256, host side). A
  second device that has the same value derives the same key, so it opens the same copy and **no key
  ever travels** between devices.
- **So the plugin and its service CAN read the synced data**: the derivation is public and your code
  reads that setting; a service that issued the token (Telegram, for a bot token) can too. The consent
  sheet says so in **one red line**, the same for every provider: "Sincronizará tus datos a través de su
  servicio: el plugin y su servicio podrán leerlos" ("Will sync your data through its service: the
  plugin and its service can read it"). An update that adds the capability always waits for the
  person's approval.
- Say it plainly in your plugin's description and guide too: whoever holds the token can read the data.

What is inside the copy: everything Kino already syncs between paired devices over the local network,
the same rows (library, history, progress, settings, the installed plugins and their settings), for
every profile this device syncs. Plugin passwords and the other secrets Kino syncs are in it too, each
still sealed row by row with the sync key. Secrets sealed in a plugin's manifest never travel, as always.

## The contract { #contract }

Declare the capability (it may be the only one) and `"apiVersion": 12`, and export two functions, plus
an optional third. From `apiVersion` 13 a provider may also declare `socket`, `storageLarge`, `catalog` and
`qrScan` next to `syncProvider` and still need no `resolve`, `search` or `home` (`["syncProvider", "socket"]`
for a provider that talks over [`kino.ws`](bytes.md)); any other capability next to them brings those back.

```json
"apiVersion": 12,
"capabilities": ["syncProvider"],
"hosts": ["api.example.com"],
"sync": { "mode": "poll", "maxBlobBytes": 4194304, "keySecret": "token", "provision": ["token"] }
```

```js
export async function syncPull({ maxBlobBytes }) {
  const r = await kino.fetch(API + "/blob", { headers: auth() });
  if (r.status === 404) return null;                       // nothing stored yet
  if (r.status === 401) throw kino.error("auth_required", "token refused");
  if (!r.ok) throw kino.error("unavailable", "pull " + r.status);
  return { blob: r.json().blob, version: r.json().version };
}

export async function syncPush({ maxBlobBytes, blob, expectedVersion }) {
  const r = await kino.fetch(API + "/blob", { method: "PUT", headers: { ...auth(), "If-Match": expectedVersion ?? "" },
    body: { json: { blob } } });
  if (r.status === 409) throw kino.error("conflict", "the stored copy changed");
  if (!r.ok) throw kino.error("unavailable", "push " + r.status);
  return { version: r.json().version };
}

export async function syncStatus(_null) {                  // optional
  if (!kino.config.get("token")) return { ready: false, message: "Falta el token: escríbelo en Configurar" };
  return { ready: true };
}
```

- **One argument, an object** (`null` for `syncStatus`). `maxBlobBytes` is the manifest's value (at most
  4194304).
- **`blob`** is standard base64 (RFC 4648, `+` and `/`, padded) **without line breaks**, in both
  directions. Store it and give it back byte for byte; never decode it into text. A pull answers
  `{ blob, version }`, or `null` when nothing is stored yet.
- **`version`** is a non-blank string of yours (an ETag, a message id, a counter). Kino hands the last one
  it pulled back to `syncPush` as `expectedVersion` (`null` when it pulled nothing).
- **Conflicts.** If your service can tell that the remote copy changed since `expectedVersion`, throw
  `kino.error("conflict", "…")`: Kino pulls, merges and pushes again, at most 3 more times per round.
  If it cannot tell (no compare-and-set), ignore `expectedVersion`: the merge of the next round heals
  the race.
- **Setup missing.** Throw `auth_required` from `syncPull`/`syncPush` when the plugin lacks its settings
  or the service refuses the credentials: the person reads "al proveedor le falta configuración,
  revísala en Configurar" instead of a generic failure.
- **`syncStatus`** answers `{ ready, message? }` for the provider's row. Before every round Kino asks
  it: `ready: false` skips the round (no failure, no back-off, pending changes kept) and Kino asks again
  one pull period later, when the person opens the screen, or right after they save your settings. A
  missing export means ready. A `syncStatus` that throws `auth_required` also means not ready; any other
  failure of it shows the provider as not ready but lets the round run and fail on its own. Never
  download the blob in it: one cheap request at most.
- **Time**: `syncPull` and `syncPush` 60 s each, `syncStatus` 15 s. They run in the background: nobody
  waits on screen, and their timeouts never mark your plugin as "No responde". Every rule of
  `kino.fetch`, hosts and the engine applies as in any other call, except the size caps below.
- **Errors**: use the usual [`kino.error` codes](contract.md#errors); `conflict` is the one of its own. A
  `userMessage` follows the [usual rules](contract.md#user-message), so a sentence that names a token or
  a brand on the blocked list (Telegram, for example) shows as Kino's own line.
- The TypeScript shapes are `KinoSyncPullFn`, `KinoSyncPushFn`, `KinoSyncStatusFn`, `KinoSyncContext` and
  `KinoManifestSync` in [`kino.d.ts`](reference/index.md).

## The `sync` block of the manifest { #sync-block }

From `apiVersion` 12, **required** with the `syncProvider` capability and only with it (otherwise the
manifest is refused: `The "sync" field needs the "syncProvider" capability`; a provider without it or
without `keySecret`: `The "syncProvider" capability needs a "sync" field whose "keySecret" is the key of one
of the plugin's own "password" settings`). `keySecret` and `provision` are required; the rest is optional:

| Key | Default | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | `"poll"` | `"poll"` or `"realtime"` ([cadence](#cadence)) |
| `pullEveryMs` | 600000 (10 min) | a positive whole number; Kino raises it to at least 30 s |
| `pushDebounceMs` | 300000 (5 min) | a positive whole number; Kino raises it to at least 5 s |
| `maxBlobBytes` | 4194304 | the largest blob your service accepts, at most 4194304 (4 MiB) |
| `keySecret` | **required** | the `key` of one of your own `password` settings, which must not have a `default` |
| `provision` | **required** | at most 8 different keys of your own settings that hold a value (secret or not); must include `keySecret`; from apiVersion 13 it may name a `"sync": false` password ([one-shot](#one-shot)), never a `"sync": false` text |
| `generateKey` | `false` | apiVersion 13: `true` makes Kino create the `keySecret` value itself ([below](#generate-key)) |

The messages Kino gives for a malformed block (all in English, shown at install):

- `The "sync" field must be an object with an optional "mode" of "poll" or "realtime" and optional positive whole numbers "pullEveryMs", "pushDebounceMs" and "maxBlobBytes" (at most 4194304)`
- `The "keySecret" of the "sync" field must be the key of one of the plugin's own "password" settings`
- `The setting the "keySecret" of the "sync" field names must not have a "default"`
- `The "provision" of the "sync" field must be a list of at most 8 different keys of the plugin's own settings that hold a value`
- `The "provision" of the "sync" field must include its "keySecret"`
- `The "keySecret" of the "sync" field can't name a setting with "sync": false` (apiVersion 13)
- `The "provision" of the "sync" field can't name a text setting with "sync": false` (apiVersion 13)
- `The "generateKey" of the "sync" field must be true or false` (apiVersion 13)

**`keySecret`** must be a **long random token** (a bot token, an API key, a token your server prints),
never a password a person picks: anyone who gets a stored blob can try guesses offline. Until the person
types it Kino runs no round (the card names the setting by its label, "Falta «Clave de sincronización»: ve a
Configurar"; a label with "token" reads "Falta el token"). Changing its value
changes the key: the remote copy then no longer opens ("El token no coincide o los datos guardados no
son de Kino", with "Corregir el token" and "Restablecer sincronización") until the person corrects the token
or resets sync on one device. Every other device needs the new value too ("Enviar configuración", or typed).

**`provision`** names what "Enviar configuración" hands to a second device ([below](#provisioning)).
Name everything the second device needs to run the same provider (for Telegram, the bot token **and**
the chat id), and nothing it does not.

### A key Kino makes (`generateKey`, apiVersion 13) { #generate-key }

A provider whose service gives no shared secret of its own (the person's own account, not a bot token)
declares `"generateKey": true`. Kino then makes the `keySecret` value itself: 32 random bytes from a
`SecureRandom`, as 64 lower-case hex characters, only while that setting is empty and at two moments:
when the person switches the provider on, and when they press "Enviar configuración" (the key is made
before the values are read, so an empty key never hides that button: it shows as soon as your other
`provision` settings hold values). It is saved exactly like a typed password (sealed, synced end to end,
per profile), never logged, and never drawn in your form on any device. A value that exists, typed or
received, is never replaced; a value received from another device always replaces a generated one. Your
plugin needs no "Create key" action. Below apiVersion 13 the key is ignored.

```json
"sync": { "keySecret": "syncKey", "generateKey": true, "provision": ["syncKey", "api_id", "api_hash"] }
```

Older Kino builds refuse `apiVersion` 12 ("Este plugin necesita una versión más nueva de Kino").

## When rounds run { #cadence }

A round is pull, merge, push. With `mode: "poll"` Kino runs one:

- when the app comes to the front, then every `pullEveryMs` while it stays there;
- `pushDebounceMs` after the **last** local change (a burst of changes is one push), and never sooner
  than that after the previous round; going to the background sends a pending push at once;
- for the playback position, when playback stops or the app goes to the background, never while it
  advances;
- when the person taps "Sincronizar ahora" ("Sync now").

`pullEveryMs` is only the default: each provider's card in Sincronización ▸ Proveedor has **"Sincronizar
cada"** (1, 5, 10, 30 or 60 minutes, starting at your value rounded to the nearest one), chosen per device
and never synced. Your plugin is not told and needs nothing for it; the push debounce stays yours.

There are at most 60 rounds in any hour, whatever asks. A failed round waits the pull interval doubled
per consecutive failure (up to 30 minutes); the changes it carried stay pending.

**`mode: "realtime"`** keeps all of that and adds one signal: when your code learns that another device
stored a new copy, it calls [`kino.sync.remoteChanged()`](kino-api.md#sync) and Kino pulls at once.
Kino accepts at most one signal every 30 seconds and drops one that arrives during a pull. Your code only
runs while Kino calls it (no open connection between calls), so the place to notice a change is
`syncStatus`, not `syncPull`.

## Size limits { #limits }

- The blob is at most `sync.maxBlobBytes` (4 MiB at most) **decoded**. Kino refuses a larger one in both
  directions: a snapshot bigger than your limit is refused before it reaches you ("tus datos superan el
  tamaño que admite el proveedor"), and a pulled blob over it is not applied.
- Inside `syncPull` and `syncPush` **only**, a `kino.fetch` request (its JSON, the base64 body included)
  and a response body may reach ceil(`maxBlobBytes` × 4/3) + 64 KB instead of 1 MB and 5 MB, and so may
  the call's answer, so the base64 blob fits in one request. Every other call of the plugin keeps the
  usual caps; hosts, budgets, redirects and timeouts do not change.
- Why 4 MiB: the blob crosses the engine as base64 text several times. At 4 MiB a provider needs about
  25 to 30 MB of the plugin's 64 MB engine memory, so keep your own data small while those calls run and
  never build extra copies of the blob (see how Sync-Gram builds a multipart body without decoding it).
- Declare what your service really takes: a smaller `maxBlobBytes` also keeps the raised caps small.

## Sending the settings to another device { #provisioning }

The person configures the provider on one device (the first one never needs a QR). For the second,
Kino carries the settings your manifest names in `sync.provision`, encrypted end to end from one Kino
to the other (to a key the receiving device makes for this one session):

1. On the **second** device (say, the TV): the provider's card ▸ **"Recibir configuración"**
   ("Receive settings"). For 3 minutes it shows a QR, an address on the local network and a
   6-digit code. In parallel it tries to open a **second route over the internet** ("Desde otra red", a
   Cloudflare quick tunnel); when it comes up, the screen also shows a few hyphenated **words** (the
   tunnel's name). The QR waits for the tunnel at most a few seconds, then shows the local network only.
2. On the **first** device: the same card ▸ **"Enviar configuración"** ("Send settings"). It
   scans the QR, which lists the local-network addresses first and then
   `https://<words>.trycloudflare.com/t/<token>`; the phone tries the local addresses first, then the
   tunnel. Without a camera, or with the camera refused, it goes to **"Escribir dirección"**: **"Misma
   red"** (the person types only the last number of the address) or **"Otra red"** (only the words;
   Kino fills in `https://` and `.trycloudflare.com`), plus the 6-digit code. The phone accepts only those
   two shapes, so a typo cannot send the settings anywhere else.
3. The second device asks **"Recibido para <plugin>: ¿aplicar?"** and lists the settings by their
   labels, never secret values (a `url` setting shows its address, with a warning when it is on the local
   network). Only **Aplicar** saves them.

**What protects the internet route, plainly.** The tunnel's words are **public**: the TV screen, the
sender's DNS query and TLS name, and Cloudflare all see them. The `/t/<token>` path in the QR is defence
in depth only (the typed route reaches the same session without it). The real gate, on every route, is
the 6-digit code (plus, on a typed route, the receiver's key masked by that code), with **5 attempts** in
all, of which at most 3 can come through the tunnel (after the third, only the tunnel closes and the
local network keeps its attempts), a **single** valid message, a **3-minute** life, a ceiling of **40
requests** on the tunnel, and the person's "¿aplicar?". The transport is never trusted. The residual risk
is a denial of service: anyone who has the words can spend the tunnel's attempts and close that route.

**About the tunnel.** It is the owner's
[cloudflare-quick-tunnel-kotlin](https://github.com/kinotvapp/cloudflare-quick-tunnel-kotlin) library,
built into the app and loaded only when a receiving screen opens. It uses TCP 7844 (TLS 1.3 + HTTP/2) to
Cloudflare's edge, no QUIC; it asks `api.trycloudflare.com` for a tunnel and resolves the edge through
public DNS (1.1.1.1, 1.0.0.1, 8.8.8.8). Cloudflare's quick tunnels are anonymous and meant for testing and
development: no uptime guarantee, they can be rate-limited ("Cloudflare está limitando las rutas por
internet…"), and a network that blocks them leaves the local route only. Your plugin has nothing to do
with any of it.

What this means for your plugin:

- Only the settings in `sync.provision` travel, sealed like typed ones; anything else is refused. The
  sync key never travels: each device derives it from the same token. Received values are saved like
  typed ones but, as with an action's `setSettings`, Kino does **not** run your `validateSettings` on them.
- "Enviar configuración" is offered only when this device holds a value for every setting in
  `provision`, except a key Kino makes ([`generateKey`](#generate-key): made at that moment) and a
  [one-shot](#one-shot) device-only password (left out while blank). Fill the ones you find yourself (a
  chat id) with [`setSettings`](settings-form.md#set-settings), so the person never types them; from
  apiVersion 13 `setSettings` may fill a password too.
- **The card follows the provider's state.** On a device that does not hold the `provision` values it
  needs yet, your card leads with "Recibir configuración" (with one line saying how) and "Configurar"
  turns quiet. On the TV: nothing received yet, only "Recibir configuración"; received but not set up
  (the key is missing, your `syncStatus` says not ready, or the last round needed setup), "Configurar"
  and a quiet "Recibir"; ready, "Sincronizar cada" and a quiet "Recibir". The TV never names a setting
  for a missing key: it says to receive the setup from another device, so write your own TV lines the
  same way.
- The plugin must already be installed on the receiving device ("Instala primero <plugin>").
- With no route at all, the person types the same settings in the second device's own form, unless
  your plugin draws them on the phone only ([`devices`](settings-form.md#devices)): then receiving them
  is the TV's way.

### A one-shot secret for the new device (apiVersion 13) { #one-shot }

`provision` may also name a password with [`"sync": false`](settings-form.md#sync-false), for a secret the
new device needs **once** (a two-step verification password, so the TV never types it). It goes only while
it holds a value on the sending device: blank (already used and cleared), it is left out and never stops
the rest from going. The sending screen adds a plain line naming it by its label ("También se envía:
Contraseña 2FA. En el otro aparato queda solo ahí: no se sincroniza ni entra en las copias de seguridad." /
"Also sent: 2FA password. On the other device it stays there only: it never syncs or goes into backups.");
the receiving device lists its label only, never the value, and stores it sealed and device-only exactly
as if typed there: never synced, never in a backup. Your plugin clears it itself once used (an action's
`clearSettings`). Never use it for a lasting secret, and never as `keySecret` (refused). A `"sync": false`
**text** (a phone number kept on the device) can never be in `provision`.

## Settings, profiles and what the person reads { #settings }

- **Configurar** ("Set up") on the provider's card opens your plugin's own settings form. Use the
  [configuration aids](settings-form.md#aids): a short `help` (what the person needs and where to get
  it) and a `link` to the place they get it (`https://t.me/BotFather`, your guide). Use
  [`action.link`](settings-form.md#link) when an action finds **who** to link ("¿Eres tú, @ana?") and
  [`setSettings`](settings-form.md#set-settings) to store what it found. A sign-in in steps can hide what
  the current step does not need with [`settingsStatus` `hide`](settings-form.md#status-hide) (apiVersion 13).
- The provider is per device, but its calls run with the settings of the **profile in use**, the same
  ones the derived key comes from. A profile without the token shows "Este perfil no tiene el token";
  two profiles with different tokens read each other's copy as the wrong key. Tell the person to set the
  provider up in the profile they use.
- The row shows Kino's own lines ("Sincronizado hace 3 min", "Esperando la primera sincronización",
  "Falló la última sincronización: …") and, under them, your `syncStatus` `message`, scrubbed of your
  secrets. When a round fails, the person reads one of Kino's reasons, not your error text: put what
  the person must do in the `message` of `syncStatus`.
- Never put a token in an error, a status line or a log. Kino scrubs your stored secrets from what it
  shows and logs only the host of each plugin request, but a value you build yourself (a token-shaped
  string from the service's own error) is yours to remove.

## Security notes { #security }

- **The `keySecret` trade-off.** Derived keys make a second device easy (same token, nothing else) at
  the cost of confidentiality toward the plugin and the service. Say so plainly in your description and
  your guide; the consent line already says it in red.
- **Revoking the token.** If a token leaks or a device is lost, the person revokes it at the service
  (for Telegram, `/revoke` in @BotFather), types the new one on one device, and taps **"Restablecer
  sincronización"** ("Reset sync"): after a confirmation, that device's copy replaces the unreadable one,
  encrypted with the new key. Then they give the other devices the new token ("Enviar configuración", or
  typed on each). Document these steps in your guide.
- **Reset sync** replaces the remote copy with this device's, with the token it has now; it never deletes
  data on the device. Kino's confirmation says so: "Se reemplaza la copia guardada en <name> por la de
  este aparato, con el token que tienes ahora. Tus otros aparatos siguen sincronizando si usan el mismo
  token; si lo cambiaste, pásales el nuevo con «Enviar configuración» o escríbelo en cada uno."
- **The service can withhold or delete the copy**, and whoever holds the token can read it or write a
  new one. A blob that does not decrypt with the device's key is refused, never applied.
- **Hosts.** `"hosts"` lists what your code reaches. A provider for a server the person runs at an
  address you cannot know needs a [`url` setting](manifest.md#own-servers) or `"fetchHosts": "any"` (red
  consent, public `https` only, never the home network): Sync Servidor uses `fetchHosts` with a `text`
  setting it validates itself.
- **Tunnels.** A plugin never reaches the home network. A server on the person's own computer needs a
  public `https` address in front of it (a Cloudflare tunnel, for example), and the person should know
  who runs that address.

## Test it locally { #test }

- `node sdk/validate.mjs .` checks the `sync` block exactly as Kino does and prints the consent line
  (always red).
- `sdk/run.mjs` has no command for the sync exports. Test them with `node --test`, as the examples do:
  load the plugin with `loadPlugin` (`sdk/sandbox.mjs`) and `createKino` (`sdk/kino-shim.mjs`), run it
  against a local imitation of your service, and check every answer with `checkSyncAnswer`
  (`sdk/contract.mjs`). Include a 4 MiB blob both ways and a conflict.
- On a device: turn the provider on, Configurar, a first round, a change on each device, a wrong token,
  "Restablecer sincronización", and "Enviar configuración" to a second device.

## The three example providers { #examples }

All three are public repositories you can read, copy or use as a template, each with a guide in English and
Spanish that a person can follow end to end, and tests that need no network.

- **Sync-Gram**, [kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-gram](https://github.com/kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-gram)
  (id `sync-gram`; unofficial, not affiliated with Telegram): a Telegram
  bot the person creates with @BotFather. `"hosts": ["api.telegram.org"]` only; the copy is a document
  pinned in the person's private chat with the bot (`sendDocument`, `pinChatMessage`, `getChat` for the
  version and a race check, `getFile` to read it back). It shows a multipart upload through `kino.fetch`
  without decoding the blob, linking the chat with `getUpdates` and `action.link`, the confirmed chat
  saved with `setSettings`, a short `help` and a `link` to @BotFather, and every error scrubbed of the
  token. `keySecret` is the bot token and `provision` is `["botToken", "chatId"]`. Its setup is
  `"devices": ["phone"]` with numbered section titles, and its confirm action is `linkOnly`. It is the
  reference for a provider on a third-party service. It is signed and listed in Kino's recommended
  plugins from Kino 0.9.74 (`requires: ["syncProvider"]`, so older Kino never shows it).
- **Sync Servidor**, [kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-server](https://github.com/kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-server)
  (id `sync-server`): a single-file Node server with no dependencies
  (`GET /blob`, `PUT /blob` with `If-Match`, a 409 on a version mismatch, a bearer token) and the plugin
  that talks to it (`"fetchHosts": "any"`, `keySecret` and `provision`, a 409 thrown as `conflict`), reached
  through a Cloudflare tunnel. It is the reference for a provider on the person's own server. It is
  **not listed** in Kino: people install it by pasting its repository address,
  `kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-server/plugin` (signed), or their own server's
  `https://<address>/plugin/kino-plugin.json`.
- **Sync-Gram Cuenta**, [kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-gram-account](https://github.com/kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-gram-account)
  (id `sync-gram-account`, apiVersion 13, Kino 0.9.74 or newer; unofficial, not affiliated with Telegram):
  the person's **own Telegram account**, no bot. The copy is one file, `kino-sync.bin`, pinned and sent
  silently in their Saved Messages, through Telegram's MTProto API over `kino.ws`
  (`"capabilities": ["syncProvider", "socket", "storageLarge"]`, the five `*.web.telegram.org` hosts only).
  The person brings their own `api_id` and `api_hash` from my.telegram.org. It is the reference for the
  apiVersion 13 additions: [`generateKey`](#generate-key) (no "Create key" step), a [one-shot](#one-shot)
  two-step password sent once to the TV, a phone number as a [`"sync": false` text](settings-form.md#sync-false),
  [`settingsStatus` `hide`](settings-form.md#status-hide) by sign-in stage, and a [`qr`](qr.md) login drawn
  on the TV only. The phone signs in with its number and a code; the TV receives the settings with
  "Recibir configuración" and then shows a QR to scan with Telegram on the phone. It is signed and **not
  listed** in Kino: people install it by pasting its repository address,
  `kinotvapp/kino-plugin-sync-gram-account`.


<!-- page: https://kinotvapp.github.io/kino-plugins/en/plugin-stores/ (docs/plugin-stores.en.md) -->

# Plugin stores { #plugin-stores }

!!! note "Available with Kino 0.9.77"
    `pluginStore` is `apiVersion` 15 and arrives with Kino 0.9.77, together with
    [`identity`](identity.md) and [`notifications`](notifications.md). An older version refuses these plugins with
    «Este plugin necesita una versión más nueva de Kino».

A plugin that declares **`pluginStore`** is a **source of plugins** for Kino's store: it hands Kino a list of plugins people
can install, and Kino does everything else. Anyone can publish a store, backed by GitHub, by their own server or by a static
JSON file.

The author of a plugin answers for it; **Kino only lists what stores hand it**. A store never installs anything by itself:
installing is always Kino's own flow (preview, consent sheet, install).

## How it fits together { #how }

- **Kino paints the store, not the plugin.** Kino keeps one **local index** holding the entries of every store, each row
  tagged with its store, and the Plugins screen reads only that index: cards, search, categories, sort and pagination are
  local queries, instant and the same with no network.
- **Your plugin only hands over entries.** It syncs (`storeSync`) in the background and, if it is a live store, answers
  while the person browses (`storeList`, `storeSearch`). It draws nothing.
- **Three tabs.** The store view has "From Kino", "Community" and "Installed" (in Spanish: «De Kino», «De la comunidad»,
  «Instalados»). "From Kino" is Kino Plugins' default list. "Community" is everything else, from every store, **without Kino's
  list**: it has the sort («Populares» or «Recientes»), the store filter and the live stores.
- **Every card says where it came from**: at the bottom, the store's icon and «de <store name>». At the top there is a
  store filter: «Todas las tiendas» (the default), then every installed and active store.
- **Kino Plugins** is the store that ships in the app: an ordinary, signed plugin that cannot be uninstalled (it can be
  switched off). It is the worked example of a local store: see [below](#kino-plugins).

## The manifest { #manifest }

```json
{
  "id": "ana-store", "name": "Ana's store", "version": "1.0.0", "apiVersion": 15, "entry": "plugin.js",
  "hosts": ["plugins.ana.example"],
  "capabilities": ["pluginStore"],
  "pluginStore": { "mode": "local", "name": "Ana's store" }
}
```

- `pluginStore` (the capability) needs `apiVersion: 15`, **may be declared alone** (a store plays nothing, so it needs
  neither `resolve` nor `search`), is not offered through [`enhancements`](enhancements.md) and needs the person's approval
  at install and on the update that adds it.
- The `pluginStore` block is optional: `mode` is `"local"` (the default) or `"live"`, and `name` (1 to 60 characters) is how
  the store shows in the filter and on its cards (default: the plugin's `name`). The block without the capability is refused.
- `hosts`: your store reaches only the hosts you declare, like any plugin.
- **One plugin per `id`.** Do not use the id `kino-plugins`: it is Kino's own store and no store may list it. And when two
  repositories claim the same `id` across all stores, only one stays: the one in Kino Plugins' list or, if none is there, one
  picked deterministically (see [how Kino mixes stores](#mixing)).

## `storeSync`: every store { #store-sync }

```js
export async function storeSync({ reason, since, state }) {
  // reason: "schedule" (the background refresh) or "reload" (the person pressed reload)
  // since:  when this store last synced successfully, in ms (absent the first time, and when Kino lost your rows)
  // state:  what you returned as `state` last time (at most 16 KB of JSON; also absent in those cases)
  const r = await kino.fetch("https://plugins.ana.example/list.json");
  return { full: true, entries: r.json().plugins.map(toEntry), state: { etag: "…" } };
}
```

It answers `{ full, entries, removed?, state? }`:

| Answer | What Kino does |
| --- | --- |
| `full: true` | `entries` is the **whole** list: Kino replaces your store's rows; anything missing is removed. |
| `full: false` | `entries` are additions or changes and `removed` the addresses that left: Kino applies them. An empty change (`entries: []`) means "nothing changed". |
| `state` | A small object (a cursor, an etag, the date of your last index) that Kino keeps and hands back on the next call. |

How you get the list (GitHub, your server, a static file) is your business. `storeSync` runs **only in the background**, at the
interval the person chooses (every 2 hours by default, Wi-Fi only), and when they press the reload icon; nothing waits for it
while they browse. A store that fails 3 times in a row pauses until the next reload.

**Be ready for `since` to be absent at any time.** If Kino loses your store's rows (a restore, a rebuilt database), it syncs the
store again from scratch: no `since` and no `state`, just like the first time. Your `storeSync` must then answer its **whole**
list (`full: true`) and not assume it has a saved cursor.

## An entry (`StoreEntry`) { #entry }

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `address` | What Kino installs from: `owner/repo`, `owner/repo/path`, `owner/repo@ref` or `url:https://…/kino-plugin.json`. Required unless there is `stremio`. |
| `id` | The plugin's `id` (its `kino-plugin.json`'s). Required. |
| `name` | 1 to 60 characters. Required. |
| `description`, `longDescription` | Up to 300 and up to 4000 characters. |
| `categories` | `movies`, `series`, `anime`, `live`, `radio`, `subtitles`, `utilities`, `themes`, `adult`, or a new type (`manga`, `audio-books`: 2 to 24 lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter; its chip is the id with hyphens as spaces and a capital first letter). |
| `tags`, `icon`, `screenshots` | Up to 10 tags of 30 characters; the icon and up to 8 screenshots, `https` only and from a public host (never an IP address, `localhost`, a name without a dot or a local-network name). |
| `version`, `author` | Short text (40 and 60 characters). |
| `popularity`, `updatedAt` | Numbers: for the «Populares» and «Recientes» sorts of "Community" (`updatedAt` in ms). |
| `stremio`, `requires`, `needsSetup` | A Stremio addon installs through Kino's Stremio flow (then `address` may be absent); `requires` lists capabilities this Kino must be able to run, or the entry is hidden; `needsSetup` says it asks for configuration. |
| `signed`, `authorKey` | **Hints**: the card says «Firmado», and an installed plugin with that id pinned to that author key (64 lowercase hex characters) reads as installed. Kino re-checks at install. |
| `recommended` | Kino honours it **only** from Kino Plugins, and it is what puts the entry in "From Kino"; from any other store it is ignored. |

An entry with no `address` and no `stremio`, no valid `id` or no `name` is dropped; long texts are cut; an icon or screenshot that is not `https` on a public host (an IP address, `localhost`, a name
without a dot or with a local suffix such as `.local`) is dropped. Past 5000 entries (counting only valid ones, repeats of an address skipped) the rest are dropped. Kino never trusts
a store's hints.

## Local and live { #modes }

| | **Local** store (default) | **Live** store (`"mode": "live"`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exports | `storeSync` | `storeSync`, `storeList` and `storeSearch` (all three) |
| While the person browses | Never touches the network | Answers what its synced list lacks |
| What the person reads at install | One plain line: «Agrega plugins de sus servidores a tu tienda» ("Adds plugins from its servers to your store") | That one and, **in red**: «Lo que busques en la tienda llegará a sus servidores» ("What you search in the store will reach its servers") |

```js
// A live store: besides storeSync
export async function storeList({ category, sort, cursor }) { /* sort: "popular" | "recent" */ return { entries, next }; }
export async function storeSearch({ q, category, cursor }) { return { entries, next }; }
```

Each answers `{ entries, next? }`, at most **50 entries a page** (`kinoStore.limits.maxEntriesPerLivePage`; the rest are dropped); `next` is the cursor of the following page. A call takes **at most 5 s** and a store gets
**20 calls a minute**: past either, that call adds nothing. Kino keeps a live page for about **30 minutes**, tagged as live
cache: going back to the same search or page shows it at once, and those rows never count as the store's synced list.

### How Kino mixes stores { #mixing }

1. **A store may be both.** A live store should also sync a base list (its featured or newest entries) so it shows up at once
   and offline; live calls only add what that base lacks.
2. **Stable order.** In «Todas las tiendas» local entries come first, in the chosen order; a live store's results are
   **appended at the end** as they arrive. Nothing already on screen moves and focus (on a TV) never jumps.
3. **No repeats.** A live entry whose address is already in the list is skipped; the same address from two stores shows once
   (Kino Plugins' copy first). **One repository per `id`, across all stores:** the one in Kino Plugins' list wins; if none is
   there, Kino keeps one deterministically. And no store may list the id `kino-plugins`. "Community" leaves out what "From
   Kino" shows, whichever store lists it, so a live store only answers there.
4. **One «Cargar más».** It pages through the local index first, then asks each live store for its next page.
5. **Search.** Local results update as the person types; live searches wait until typing stops (half a second) and a newer
   search cancels an older one.
6. **A live store picked in the filter** shows **only** its live answers, nothing local.

## What Kino does by itself { #kino-does }

- **The blocklist.** Kino applies its blocklist (`community-blocklist.json`, see [Claims and plugin takedowns](claims.md)) to
  **every entry of every store** before painting, and again at install. Stores neither receive nor apply it: because Kino
  paints, no store can show a blocked plugin. Kino refreshes that list with every store sync (and on reload), and Kino Plugins'
  daily index already leaves blocked repositories out.
- **The 18+ code.** While the person's 18+ code is locked, an entry whose categories include `adult`, or that Kino already
  knows as 18+, is hidden from "From Kino", "Community", search, the detail sheet and the counts, from every store; a store whose
  own plugin is 18+ is not offered in the filter. Unlocking shows them. Installing one goes through the usual 18+ gate.
- **Plugins that disappear.** A repository that is deleted or loses the topic leaves its store's next list; a plugin whose
  manifest answers 404 when viewed or installed is dropped at once. Leaving a store **never uninstalls** anything: an
  installed plugin keeps working and Instalados says «Ya no está en ninguna tienda».
- **Switching a store off.** A store is switched off from its tab in Ajustes (and uninstalled like any plugin, except Kino
  Plugins), where its interval is also set; its rows leave the index at once.
- **Reloading.** The store view has a reload icon that syncs every active store now. When it ends, a toast says
  "N plugins updated" (Spanish: «Se actualizaron N plugins») or, if nothing changed, "Your plugins are up to date" («Tus plugins están al día»).
- **Installing.** Always the installer: address preview, consent sheet («Plugin no verificado…» when it is not signed) and
  install. Nothing installs by itself.

## Limits { #limits }

| What | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Entries per `storeSync` | 5000 (the rest are dropped) |
| Entries per page of a live store | 50 (the rest are dropped) |
| Size of a `storeSync` answer | 4 MB of JSON |
| `state` | 16 KB of JSON |
| One `storeSync` run | 60 s, 40 `kino.fetch` requests and 8 MB downloaded (more than a scheduled job) |
| Live calls (`storeList`, `storeSearch`) | 5 s each, 20 a minute per store; a 30-minute cache |

The exact numbers are in `contract.json` (`kinoStore.limits`).

## Two example stores { #examples }

Two complete, copyable plugins, validated with the kit and with tests that run without a network:
[**Example stores**](store-examples.md): a **local** store whose list is a static JSON file and a **live** store with its own
API. And to start yours:

```
node sdk/init.mjs my-store --host plugins.ana.example --store local     # or --store live
```

## Kino Plugins: the store that ships in the app { #kino-plugins }

**Kino Plugins** (`kinotvapp`, signed with Kino's author key) is an ordinary **local** store, with a single capability,
`pluginStore`, and the hosts `api.github.com`, `raw.githubusercontent.com`, `cdn.jsdelivr.net` and `archive.org`. It
ships inside Kino and is signed with Kino's author key (version 1.0.2). What its `storeSync` answers:

1. **The first time**, with no network: the list the plugin itself carries (the plugins Kino Plugins lists by default and the
   community's), so the store is full from the first start. The ones from Kino's catalog carry `recommended`.
2. **Once a day**, `index.json` from `kinotvapp/kino-plugins`: a static file that **is built every day** by a GitHub Action
   that walks the repositories with the `kino-plugin` topic. Re-reading it brings the stars and drops repositories that lost
   the topic, were deleted or are on the owner's blocklist. It applies the one-repository-per-`id` rule.
3. **Between one index and the next**, a small change (`full: false`): a GitHub search for what changed since the last time,
   keeping its cursor in `state`.

It is the pattern for a big store: a full list now and then and small changes in between. To be in that list, see
[Get listed in Kino](listed.md).

## Testing with the kit { #kit }

```
node sdk/validate.mjs <folder>                                  # the consent lines and the functions
node sdk/run.mjs <folder> storeSync [--since <ms>] [--state '<json>']
node sdk/run.mjs <folder> storeList [popular|recent] [category]     # a live store
node sdk/run.mjs <folder> storeSearch "<q>" [category]              # a live store
```

The kit prints the answer as Kino's index would keep it and tells you on stderr what Kino would drop
(`[dropped by Kino] …`). The types are in `kino.d.ts` (`StoreEntry`, `StoreSyncArg`, `StoreSyncAnswer`, `StoreListArg`,
`StoreSearchArg`) and the contract in `contract.json` (`kinoStore`). More in [Test it locally](test-locally.md#api15).

with no `since` and no `state`, and the plugin answers the whole list.

# Sockets and plugin-served bytes (`socket` and `byteSource`, apiVersion 13) { #bytes }

!!! note "Available from Kino 0.9.74"
    apiVersion 13 arrives in Kino 0.9.74, together with apiVersion 12. Every Kino before 0.9.74 refuses a manifest with
    `"apiVersion": 13` ("Este plugin necesita una versión más nueva de Kino").

Some services are not HTTP at all: a messaging service speaks its own protocol over a WebSocket, and the video lives in
messages, not behind a URL. Two capabilities cover that case. Declare either or both, with `"apiVersion": 13`:

```json
"apiVersion": 13,
"capabilities": ["search", "resolve", "socket", "byteSource"],
"hosts": ["ws.example.org"]
```

- **`socket`** gives your code `kino.ws`: outbound WebSockets (`wss://` only) to the hosts you declare.
- **`byteSource`** lets `resolve()` answer a stream that has no URL, `{ source: "plugin", handle, size, mime }`; Kino then
  asks your `read` export for its bytes, one range at a time, and plays them in its own player, on a Chromecast or on a
  DLNA TV.

Neither has a consent line of its own: `socket` reaches only the hosts the consent screen already lists, and
`byteSource` reaches nothing.

## `kino.ws`: WebSockets (`socket`) { #ws }

Declarative: nothing to export.

```js
const ws = await kino.ws.open("wss://ws.example.org/apiws", { protocol: "binary" });
await ws.send(new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]));
const reply = await ws.recv(10000);   // Uint8Array, or null when nothing came within 10 s
await ws.close();
```

- **Host rules.** `wss://` only (a plain `ws://` is refused with code `not_https`), on port 443 only, and the host must
  be one your manifest declares in `hosts` and the person approved. Anything else is refused with `host_not_allowed` (the
  error carries the `host`). Never the local network and never an IP literal, the same rule as `kino.fetch`. Opening
  never asks the person about a new host: declare it in `hosts`.
- **Limits.** At most 4 open sockets per plugin (the fifth is refused with `limit`) and at most 8 MiB of received
  messages queued unread per socket; past that the socket closes and `recv` fails with `limit` once what was queued is
  read. A frame you send is at most 786,000 bytes (a bigger one fails with `too_large`: split it). One `recv` waits at
  most 60 s (30 s when you give no time). A socket the plugin never closes lives until Kino closes the plugin's sandbox
  (idle 5 minutes), which closes every socket it opened. Messages are binary (`Uint8Array`).
- **Closed sockets.** `send` or `recv` on a closed socket fails with code `closed`; `recv` on a socket the other side
  closed answers what is still queued, then fails with `closed`. Close every socket you open.
- **Session advice.** Whatever lets you reconnect later (an authorization key, a session string) is a secret. Keep it in
  a [sealed secret](manifest.md#secrets) or `kino.storage`, never in the manifest or the logs, and never send it to a
  host you did not declare.

| Error `code` | When |
| --- | --- |
| `not_https` | The address is not `wss://`. |
| `host_not_allowed` | The host is not declared and approved, is not on port 443, is an IP literal or the local network. |
| `limit` | A fifth socket, or more than 8 MiB queued unread (the socket is then closed). |
| `closed` | The socket is closed (by you, by the other side, or by Kino). |
| `network`, `timeout` | The connection could not be made. |
| `too_large` | A frame to send over 786,000 bytes (counted decoded). |
| `invalid_request` | A malformed hex or base64 frame, or an `encoding` other than `hex` and `base64`. |

### Frames as strings: `{ encoding: "hex" | "base64" }` { #encodings }

Your plugin runs in QuickJS, an interpreter: a JavaScript loop over the bytes of a message costs real time on a phone,
about a second per MiB for the decode a `Uint8Array` needs (measured on a recent phone). A binary protocol that already
works on hex strings (most do, because `kino.crypto` takes and answers hex) should ask for its frames encoded instead.
Kino then encodes what `recv` answers and decodes what `send` passes in native code, and no JavaScript touches the
bytes:

```js
const ws = await kino.ws.open("wss://ws.example.org/apiws", { protocol: "binary" });
await ws.send("efefefef", { encoding: "hex" });                  // 4 bytes, decoded by Kino
const hex = await ws.recv(10000, { encoding: "hex" });          // "0a1b..." (lower case), or null after 10 s
await ws.send("AAECAw==", { encoding: "base64" });              // bytes 0, 1, 2, 3
const b64 = await ws.recv(10000, { encoding: "base64" });       // padded base64, or null
await ws.close();
```

- Without `encoding` nothing changes: `recv` answers a `Uint8Array` and `send` takes one.
- `hex` is an even number of digits (either case going out, lower case coming in); `base64` is the standard alphabet,
  padded, with no whitespace. Anything else, and any other `encoding`, fails with `invalid_request` before a byte is
  sent.
- Every limit counts the decoded bytes: a frame of at most 786,000 bytes is up to 1,572,000 hex characters.

## `byteSource`: a stream the plugin serves { #byte-source }

`resolve()` answers a stream that has no URL:

```js
return { source: "plugin", handle: "msg:12345", size: 734003200, mime: "video/mp4" };
```

`handle` is yours (opaque to Kino, 1 to 512 characters), `size` is the total length in bytes and `mime` the media type.
`handle` has no control character, `size` is a positive whole number and `mime` a media type (`video/mp4`,
`video/x-matroska`...; no parameters); anything else is refused ("El video que entregó el plugin no es válido"). It is read
only from a movie's, an episode's or a track's own `resolve`, never from a live channel or a lazy alternative. The player
then asks your `read` export for the bytes, one range at a time:

```js
export async function read({ handle, offset, length }) {
  // offset is always a multiple of 4096; length is at most 1048576 (1 MiB)
  const base64 = await fetchRangeAsBase64(handle, offset, length);   // your own code
  return { bytes: base64 };                                          // the range, base64-encoded
}
```

- **Answer exactly the range asked**, or fewer bytes only when it runs past `size`. An answer that is not `{ bytes }` of
  the right length is refused as "El plugin no entregó los datos del video".
- A plugin that declares `byteSource` must export `read`, or the install fails with "El plugin no carga: le falta
  read". A `{ source: "plugin" }` answer from a plugin that does not declare the capability is refused.
- **Time.** Each `read` has 20 seconds. What it throws (or a timeout) is what the person reads when the video stops,
  worded like any other failed call. After 3 timed-out reads in a row Kino stops reading that stream until it is opened
  again (each timeout leaves your script's evaluation running until it ends by itself).
- **One at a time.** Calls to `read` come one at a time, and a call that started always runs to its end, even when the
  person seeks meanwhile, so a connection you keep open between calls stays open.
- **What the stream may carry.** A byte stream may carry `subtitles`, `audioTracks`, `durationMs`, `skip`, `label` and
  `media` like any stream; it is only for a movie, an episode or a track (never a live channel nor a lazy alternative).
- **Casting.** It casts to a Chromecast or a DLNA TV when `mime` is a video or audio file type other than MPEG-TS
  (`video/mp4`, `video/webm`, `video/x-matroska`, `audio/mpeg`...): the TV fetches it from the phone over the home
  network, from a session of its own that ends with the cast (leaving the player doesn't stop the TV), and every byte
  still comes from your `read`, which then also serves what the TV asks for. Kino never remuxes or converts it for the
  TV, so a format the TV can't play as it is won't play there.
- **No downloads.** It is never downloaded, so declaring `download` is pointless for a plugin whose streams are all
  `{ source: "plugin" }`: its titles show the download button, and every download fails as not downloadable.

### How Kino reads, and how to make it fast { #performance }

Calls to `read` are serial per plugin (one at a time, whatever the player asks), so every call's time adds up before
the first frame. Kino asks for 1 MiB per call, at an offset that is a multiple of 1 MiB, reads ahead up to 3 chunks,
keeps the last 8 chunks it read, and reads the first and the last chunk of a stream early, because a player needs both
before it can start (an MP4 whose `moov` index sits at the end, a Matroska file's cues). When the person seeks, chunks
queued for the old position are dropped and the new position goes first; a read already running still ends and its
chunk is kept. What makes a chunk fast is your own per-call time:

- **Prefer few large reads**: answer the whole `length` asked in one call; if your source serves smaller pieces, fetch
  them in parallel inside that one call rather than one after another.
- **Keep the bytes out of JavaScript loops**: take socket frames encoded (`{ encoding: "hex" }`, above), do the crypto
  with `kino.crypto` on hex, and let the last `kino.crypto` step answer `outputEncoding: "base64"` instead of converting
  in JavaScript; when the last step is not a `kino.crypto` call (bytes you sliced out of a hex message), turn them into
  base64 with `kino.crypto.convert(hex, "hex", "base64")`. A plain loop over the bytes of 1 MiB takes about a second on
  a phone.
- **Fewer big strings**: every `kino.crypto` call copies its input and its answer once each across the bridge, so one
  call that does two steps beats two calls (`kino.crypto.aesIgeVerify`, [below](#crypto)).
- Your answer's `bytes` crosses as it is: Kino reads only `bytes` (any other field of the answer is dropped), and nothing
  scans the string on its way.

**Memory.** Each open stream holds up to about 12 MiB of Kino's own memory (the chunks kept, the ones read ahead and the
one in flight), outside your 64 MB sandbox; at most 2 streams are open at once on the device, plus at most 2 served to
TVs. What your `read` builds (a hex string is 2 bytes per byte, then the base64) counts in your 64 MB: keep few chunks
of your own, and drop what you no longer need. Not measured yet on 1 GB TV boxes.

## Byte operations in `kino.crypto` (Kino 0.9.74: feature-detect) { #crypto }

For binary protocols (MTProto and the like), on strings in any of the three encodings (`utf8`, `hex`, `base64`):

```js
kino.crypto.aesIge("decrypt", keyHex, ivHex, dataHex, { keyEncoding: "hex", ivEncoding: "hex", inputEncoding: "hex", outputEncoding: "hex" })
kino.crypto.modPow(baseHex, expHex, modHex)          // big-endian hex, padded to the modulus' width
kino.crypto.gunzip(b64)                              // base64 in, text out by default
kino.crypto.convert(hex, "hex", "base64")            // re-encoding, done natively
kino.crypto.aesIgeVerify(keyHex, ivHex, dataHex, {   // AES-IGE decrypt + SHA-256 MAC check in one call
  mac: msgKeyHex, macPrefix: authKeySliceHex, macOffset: 8,
  keyEncoding: "hex", ivEncoding: "hex", inputEncoding: "hex", outputEncoding: "hex",
})
```

- `aesIge` is AES-256-IGE: a 32-byte key, a 32-byte iv (two blocks) and data a multiple of 16 bytes.
- `modPow` takes big-endian hex numbers of at most 4,096 bits and answers hex padded to the modulus' width.
- `convert(data, from, to)` turns, say, the hex of a chunk you sliced out of a message into the base64 a `read` answers,
  or a UTF-8 text into the base64 of a frame, without a JavaScript loop over its bytes.
- `aesIgeVerify` decrypts like `aesIge("decrypt", ...)` and then checks that bytes `macOffset` to
  `macOffset + mac.length` of `SHA-256(macPrefix || plaintext)` equal `mac` (`mac` and `macPrefix` read with
  `macEncoding`, hex by default). It answers the plaintext only when they match; otherwise it fails with "the mac
  doesn't match". MTProto 2.0's msg_key check is exactly that, with 32 bytes of the auth key as `macPrefix` and
  `macOffset: 8`: one call instead of a decryption, a join of the key slice with the plaintext and a hash.
- A sealed value is refused in every field of these five. Anything malformed fails with "invalid crypto operation".
- They are gated on the Kino you run on, not on your manifest: Kino gives every plugin the `kino.crypto` of its own
  version, so a Kino that predates one of them lacks it whatever `apiVersion` you declare (Kino 0.9.74 has all five, an
  older Kino none; development builds before 0.9.74 lack `convert` and `aesIgeVerify`). Feature-detect each one and keep a fallback:
  `typeof kino.crypto.convert === "function"`. The kit does the same: it offers what its own contract has. No capability
  is needed. Every `kino.crypto` call takes at most 5 MB of data.

The engine's own `atob` and `btoa` are also faster from Kino 0.9.74 (table-driven, same answers and errors), but a
1 MiB string through them is still a JavaScript-speed pass: for bulk bytes use `kino.crypto.convert`.

## A complete example: a video library behind a WebSocket { #example }

A made-up service, `files.example.org`, keeps a person's videos and speaks a tiny protocol of its own over a WebSocket:
each request is one frame of UTF-8 JSON; the answer to `{"op":"list"}` is one frame of UTF-8 JSON
(`{ "files": [{ "id", "name", "size", "mime" }] }`); the answer to `{"op":"read","id","offset","length"}` is that
range's bytes in one or more binary frames, then an empty frame. The plugin lists the files on Home and in search,
resolves a file to a byte stream, and serves it through `read`, with no JavaScript loop over the video's bytes: frames
come in as hex, are joined as strings, and become base64 natively.

`kino-plugin.json`:

```json
{
  "id": "ws-files",
  "name": "WS Files",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "apiVersion": 13,
  "entry": "plugin.js",
  "hosts": ["files.example.org"],
  "capabilities": ["home", "search", "resolve", "socket", "byteSource"]
}
```

`plugin.js`:

```js
// A video library behind a WebSocket: files.example.org (a made-up service) keeps the files and speaks a tiny protocol
// of its own. Each request is one frame of UTF-8 JSON; the answer to "list" is one frame of UTF-8 JSON; the answer to
// "read" is the range's bytes in one or more binary frames, then an empty frame.
const WS_URL = "wss://files.example.org/ws";
const WAIT_MS = 15000;

let socket = null; // module-level: kept between calls while the sandbox lives (a cache, never relied on)

async function connection() {
  if (!socket) socket = await kino.ws.open(WS_URL, { protocol: "binary" });
  return socket;
}

// Sends one request; on a socket the service closed meanwhile, opens a new one and sends it once more.
async function send(request) {
  const frame = kino.crypto.convert(JSON.stringify(request), "utf8", "base64");
  try {
    await (await connection()).send(frame, { encoding: "base64" });
  } catch (e) {
    if (e.code !== "closed") throw e;
    socket = null;
    await (await connection()).send(frame, { encoding: "base64" });
  }
}

async function nextFrame(encoding) {
  const frame = await socket.recv(WAIT_MS, { encoding });
  if (frame === null) throw kino.error("unavailable", "files.example.org did not answer in time");
  return frame;
}

async function listFiles() {
  const cached = kino.storage.get("files");
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);
  await send({ op: "list" });
  const { files } = JSON.parse(kino.crypto.convert(await nextFrame("base64"), "base64", "utf8"));
  kino.storage.set("files", JSON.stringify(files), { ttlMs: 10 * 60 * 1000 });
  return files; // [{ id, name, size, mime }]
}

const toItem = (f) => ({ id: "f" + f.id, ref: f.id, title: f.name, kind: "movie" });

export async function home() {
  const files = await listFiles();
  return [{ id: "files", title: "Mis videos", items: files.slice(0, 60).map(toItem) }];
}

export async function search(query) {
  const q = String(query.q || "").toLowerCase();
  return (await listFiles()).filter((f) => f.name.toLowerCase().includes(q)).slice(0, 100).map(toItem);
}

export async function resolve(ref) {
  const file = (await listFiles()).find((f) => f.id === ref);
  if (!file) throw kino.error("not_found", "no such file");
  // No URL: Kino plays it through read() below.
  return { source: "plugin", handle: file.id, size: file.size, mime: file.mime };
}

// Kino asks for one range at a time: offset is a multiple of 4096, length at most 1 MiB.
export async function read({ handle, offset, length }) {
  await send({ op: "read", id: handle, offset, length });
  let hex = "";
  for (;;) {
    const frame = await nextFrame("hex"); // hex string, decoded by Kino: no JavaScript loop over the bytes
    if (frame === "") break;              // the empty frame ends the range
    hex += frame;
    if (hex.length > 2 * length) throw kino.error("unavailable", "the service sent more than asked");
  }
  // Exactly the range asked, or fewer bytes only at the end of the file; base64 made natively.
  return { bytes: kino.crypto.convert(hex, "hex", "base64") };
}
```

What to notice:

- **The socket outlives a call** (module-level `socket`), because the sandbox is reused between calls; when the service
  or Kino closed it, `send` sees `closed` and opens a new one. Never rely on it surviving: Kino closes the sandbox after 5
  idle minutes, after a timeout and on an update.
- **Calls never overlap** (Kino runs one call of a plugin at a time), so one socket with one request in flight is safe
  here. A protocol that multiplexes (message ids) can keep several requests in flight inside one `read`.
- **Every byte stays a string**: hex frames joined with `+=`, then `kino.crypto.convert` to base64. A real service would
  add its own framing, retries and crypto (`kino.crypto.aesIge`/`aesIgeVerify` on the same hex) the same way.
- A real service also needs an account: keep its session in a [sealed secret](manifest.md#secrets) or `kino.storage`,
  and show a sign-in from the [settings form](settings-form.md) (for a TV, a [QR code](qr.md)).

### Test it with the kit { #testing }

The kit's `kino.ws` runs over Node's global `WebSocket` with the app's rules (wss only, declared hosts on port 443, the
4-socket and frame caps, `hex`/`base64` frames refused word for word like the app). To test without the network, swap
`globalThis.WebSocket` for a fake of your service before you load the plugin, and call your exports directly. This is
the test that ran the example above (Node 18+, the kit's `sdk/` next to it):

```js
// test/plugin.test.mjs -- node --test test/plugin.test.mjs
import test from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { createKino } from "../sdk/kino-shim.mjs";
import { loadPlugin } from "../sdk/sandbox.mjs";
import { validateManifest } from "../sdk/contract.mjs";

const FILE = Buffer.alloc(2_500_000).map((_, i) => (i * 31 + 7) & 255);

// files.example.org, faked: answers "list" and "read" as the protocol above says.
class FakeService {
  constructor() { this.l = {}; this.readyState = 0; setTimeout(() => { this.readyState = 1; this.emit("open", {}); }, 0); }
  addEventListener(n, f) { (this.l[n] ||= []).push(f); }
  emit(n, e) { (this.l[n] || []).forEach((f) => f(e)); }
  reply(bytes) { const c = Uint8Array.from(bytes); setTimeout(() => this.emit("message", { data: c.buffer }), 0); }
  send(data) {
    const req = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(data).toString("utf8"));
    if (req.op === "list") this.reply(Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ files: [{ id: "a1", name: "Vacaciones 2024", size: FILE.length, mime: "video/mp4" }] })));
    if (req.op === "read") {
      const part = FILE.subarray(req.offset, Math.min(FILE.length, req.offset + req.length));
      for (let i = 0; i < part.length; i += 300_000) this.reply(part.subarray(i, i + 300_000));
      this.reply(new Uint8Array(0));
    }
  }
  close() { this.readyState = 3; this.emit("close", {}); }
}

test("lists, resolves to a byte stream and serves every range", async () => {
  const manifestText = readFileSync(new URL("../kino-plugin.json", import.meta.url), "utf8");
  assert.equal(validateManifest(manifestText).ok, true);
  globalThis.WebSocket = FakeService;
  const { kino } = createKino(JSON.parse(manifestText));
  const { plugin } = await loadPlugin(new URL("../plugin.js", import.meta.url).pathname, kino);
  assert.equal((await plugin.home())[0].items[0].title, "Vacaciones 2024");
  const s = await plugin.resolve("a1");
  assert.deepEqual({ ...s }, { source: "plugin", handle: "a1", size: FILE.length, mime: "video/mp4" });
  for (let offset = 0; offset < FILE.length; offset += 1048576) {
    const { bytes } = await plugin.read({ handle: "a1", offset, length: 1048576 });
    assert.ok(Buffer.from(bytes, "base64").equals(FILE.subarray(offset, offset + 1048576)), "range at " + offset);
  }
});
```

**The kit's own tools.** `checkOutput("resolve", ...)` (and so `node sdk/run.mjs . resolve <ref>`) accepts the
`{ source: "plugin", handle, size, mime }` shape of a plugin that declares `byteSource`, with the rules above.
`askRead(plugin, manifest, stream, offset, length)` from `sdk/kino-shim.mjs` calls your `read` the way Kino's proxy does
(the capability and the export, an offset that is a multiple of 4,096 inside the stream, 1 to 1,048,576 bytes, one call
at a time, 20 s, exactly `min(length, size - offset)` bytes back) and resolves with a Buffer. From the terminal:

```
node sdk/run.mjs --size 2500000 . read a1 0 1048576   # the byte count, the sha256 and the first bytes
```

`node sdk/init.mjs my-plugin --host example.com --with byteSource,socket` scaffolds an apiVersion 13 plugin with a
working, commented `read` and `kino.ws` example.

!!! warning "What the kit does not reproduce"
    Kino's player side: the 1 MiB chunks, the read-ahead, the early first and last chunk, the 3-timeouts stop and the
    cast sessions. Install the plugin on a device to see it play.

See also: [the `kino` API](kino-api.md#ws), [the limits](engine-limits.md#limits), [the contract's
`Stream` rules](contract.md#stream), and [images from the plugin](images.md), which wait while a byte stream plays.


<!-- page: https://kinotvapp.github.io/kino-plugins/en/files/ (docs/files.en.md) -->

# Files on the person's device (`files`, apiVersion 21) { #files }

!!! note "Available from Kino 0.9.82"
    apiVersion 21 arrives in Kino 0.9.82. A Kino before 0.9.82 refuses a manifest with `"apiVersion": 21` ("Este plugin
    necesita una versión más nueva de Kino"). Declare 21 only if you use `files`.

A plugin that reads books, plays music or shows videos the person already keeps on their phone or TV declares `files`. The
person picks a file (or a whole folder) with Kino's own picker. The plugin gets an opaque **handle**, never an address, and
reads the file by ranges or hands it to the player. **Nothing is uploaded or sent anywhere by this capability**: the bytes
stay on the device unless your own code sends them somewhere you declared in `hosts`.

```json
{ "apiVersion": 21, "capabilities": ["screen", "files"] }
```

`files` is declarative: nothing to export. Its consent line at install is "Can keep and read the files you pick from this
device, or a whole folder if you pick one" ("Podrá guardar y leer los archivos que tú elijas de este aparato, o una carpeta
entera si la eliges"). Without the capability there is no `kino.files` (`typeof kino.files === "undefined"`). Below 21 the
manifest is refused with "The \"files\" capability needs apiVersion 21". It can stand alone (a plugin that only reads local
files needs no `search`, `home` or `resolve`), and an [enhancement](enhancements.md) may add it.

## The calls { #calls }

```js
// From a press (a screenEvent that follows a tap): the picker.
const [book] = await kino.files.pick({ kinds: ["book"] });            // [] when the person cancels
const head = await kino.files.read(book.id, { start: 0, end: 1000 });  // a Uint8Array, at most 2,000,000 bytes a call
const mine = await kino.files.list();                                  // your handles, newest first
```

| Call | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `pick({ kinds?, multiple?, copy? })` | Opens the system picker and answers the handles of what was picked (`[]` when the person cancels). `kinds` narrows what the picker offers: `video`, `audio`, `book`, `image`, `subtitle`, `other`. `copy: true` copies the bytes into your plugin's own store (up to 64 MB a file, 1 GB in all); the default keeps a **reference** (a persisted grant), which stops working if the person moves or deletes the file. |
| `pickFolder({ kinds? })` | One grant for a whole folder. List its files with `list({ folder })`. |
| `list({ folder?, kinds? })`, `folders()`, `info(id)` | What you hold, newest first: handles (`list`), the folders picked (`folders`) and one handle's record (`info`). A handle is `{ id, name, size, mime, kind, copied, addedAt, folder? }`; a folder is `{ id, name, addedAt }`. |
| `read(id, { start?, end? })`, `readText(id, { start?, end? })` | The bytes (a `Uint8Array`) or the UTF-8 text of a range, at most 2,000,000 bytes a call. A bigger file is read in several calls. |
| `forget(id)` | Drops a handle (and the copy, if the file was imported with `copy: true`). |
| `url(id)` | `kino-file:<id>`, to use as a stream's or an audio track's `url`: the player plays the file itself. The host rules do not apply to it. |

A handle is an opaque string that belongs to your plugin: another plugin cannot use it (`denied`).

## When the picker may open { #press }

`pick` and `pickFolder` only run from a settings `action`, a `panelAction` or a `screenEvent` that follows the person's own tap or
submit (the same rule as [`kino.qr.scan`](qr.md#where)). Everywhere else (Home, a search, the `open` event, a timer tick, a
`playerEvent`) they reject with `not_allowed`. Listing, reading, `info`, `url` and `forget` need no press: a handle exists only
for what the person picked.

## Playing a local file { #play }

Put `kino.files.url(id)` in a stream (`resolve`) or an audio track and the player plays the file; Kino handles seeking. A local
file is played by Kino itself: it **cannot be cast** to a Chromecast or a DLNA renderer by address, so do not offer Cast for it.

```js
export async function resolve({ ref }) {
  const id = ref.replace(/^f:/, "");
  return { streams: [{ url: kino.files.url(id), label: "On this device" }] };
}
```

## Errors { #errors }

A failed call rejects with an error whose `code` is one of:

| `code` | When | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `unavailable` | This device has no picker. | Say the feature is not available here. |
| `not_allowed` | `pick` or `pickFolder` outside a press. | Call it from the button's `screenEvent`. |
| `busy` | A picker is already open (yours or another plugin's). | Wait; do not loop. |
| `timeout` | The picker closed after 3 minutes without an answer. | Let the person try again. |
| `invalid_request` | A malformed argument. | Fix the call. |
| `gone` | The file was moved or deleted, or the grant was lost. | Say so in a line and offer to pick it again; do not show an error screen. |
| `too_large` | A `copy: true` file over the per-file limit. | Offer to keep a reference instead. |
| `denied` | The handle is not yours. | Never keep another plugin's ids. |
| `quota` | You hold too many handles, folders or copied bytes. | `forget` the ones you no longer need. |

## Limits { #limits }

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Bytes of one `read` or `readText` | 2,000,000 |
| Handles you may hold | 500 |
| Folders you may hold | 20 |
| Files read from one folder | 5,000 |
| Files in one `pick` | 50 |
| One imported file (`copy: true`) | 64 MB |
| All your imported copies | 1 GB |
| The picker stays open | 3 minutes |

- **Not synced.** A handle means nothing on another device. Sync what you save *about* a file (a reading place, a play position)
  under something that identifies the file (its name and size) and not under the handle.
- **Pictures.** To draw a book's cover, read the bytes and give an `Image` a `data:image/png;base64,…` address (see
  [Image](screen-components.md#image)).

## Test with no phone { #test }

The Node kit's `kino.files` answers from the folder named by the `KINO_FILES_DIR` environment variable (default `./.kino-files`):
`pick` hands out the files that are there, in name order. `node sdk/run.mjs` and the kit's tests exercise `pick`, `read`, `list`,
`forget` and the errors without a device; see [Test it locally](test-locally.md).

## What the person sees { #what-people-see }

Android's own file picker, opened over your screen. Kino shows no list of your handles of its own. If the file or the grant is gone
later, your next call answers `gone`.


<!-- page: https://kinotvapp.github.io/kino-plugins/en/progress/ (docs/progress.en.md) -->

# Saving where the person is (`progress`, apiVersion 22) { #progress }

!!! note "Next Kino release, not published yet"
    apiVersion 22 arrives with the next Kino release, which is not published yet. A Kino that does not have it refuses a
    manifest with `"apiVersion": 22` ("Este plugin necesita una versión más nueva de Kino"). To keep running on older Kinos,
    keep your `apiVersion` and add `progress` as an [enhancement](enhancements.md) (`enhancements["22"]`).

A plugin whose items are not videos (a manga reader, a book reader, a podcast it plays by itself) can ask Kino to remember how
far along the person is in each one. It declares `progress`, calls `kino.progress.set` as the person reads, and reads the places
back with `get` and `list`. **Kino draws nothing from it**: no Home row, no card, no screen. Your plugin builds its own shelf (a
"keep reading" row in its `home()`, a section of its screen) from what `list` answers. What Kino adds is the keeping: the places
survive a restart, follow the person between their own devices and come back with a backup.

```json
{ "apiVersion": 22, "capabilities": ["screen", "progress"] }
```

`progress` is declarative: nothing to export. It has **no consent line and no approval**: it keeps only your plugin's own data
about the person's own reading. It may stand alone, sit beside `screen` (a plugin whose only capabilities are `progress` and
`screen` is valid) or beside any other capability, and the plugin stays that kind of plugin. Without the capability there is no
`kino.progress` (`typeof kino.progress === "undefined"`).

## The calls { #calls }

```js
await kino.progress.set({ id: "ch-87", title: "Berserk", fraction: 0.4, label: "Cap. 87 · hoja 12 de 40", resume: { cap: 87, pag: 12 } });
const here = await kino.progress.get("ch-87");              // { id, fraction, title, label, labelEn?, resume: { cap: 87, pag: 12 }, done, updatedAtMs } or null
const shelf = await kino.progress.list({ limit: 15 });      // most recently set first
await kino.progress.clear("ch-87");                          // forget it
```

| Call | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `set({ id, fraction, title?, poster?, label?, labelEn?, resume?, done?, doneAt? })` | Saves where the person is in the element `id` (1 to 128 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ ~ -`, yours to choose: a chapter, a book, an episode). `fraction` is 0 to 1. Resolves when Kino has taken it, not when it is on disk. |
| `get(id)` | What you last set for it, or `null` (never set, or cleared). |
| `clear(id)` | Forgets it. |
| `list({ limit?, sinceMs? })` | Your elements, most recently set first; `limit` 1 to 100 (default 50), `sinceMs` (a finite number >= 0, milliseconds since 1970) keeps only those set at or after that time. Finished ones are included (`done: true`). |

An entry, from `get` or `list`, is `{ id, fraction, title?, poster?, label?, labelEn?, resume?, done, updatedAtMs }`: every entry
of `list` carries its `id`, and `updatedAtMs` is the time of the last `set`.

- **Optional texts.** `title` (up to 200 characters) and `poster` (an https address under the rule of a screen's
  [`Image`](screen-components.md#image), or a `KinoImageRef` of your [`imageSource`](images.md)) are for your shelf; a `set`
  that leaves them out keeps what was there. A poster that fails the rule costs only the poster. `label` and `labelEn` are one
  short line about the place, up to 80 characters each ("Cap. 87 · hoja 12 de 40"); `get` and `list` hand both back.
- **Finished.** An element is finished (`done: true`) when you say `done: true`, or, if you do not say, when `fraction` reaches
  `doneAt` (0.9 unless you give another). It stays in `list`; a later `set` with a lower fraction reopens it. An identical `set`
  changes nothing.
- **Call it as often as you like.** Even on every page turn: Kino keeps the latest `set` of each element in memory and writes to
  disk at most every 2 seconds, and always when the screen closes or the app goes to the background. More than 20 calls a second
  are coalesced, never an error.

## `resume`: your own data { #resume }

Put in `resume` whatever lets you come back to the exact place: `{ "cap": 87, "pag": 12 }`, a screen route and its arguments, a
string. It is **any JSON value** (a string, a number, a boolean, an object or an array) of up to 1024 bytes once serialized (a
longer one is refused with `too_large`). Kino stores it, syncs it and hands it back exactly as you set it, but **never reads
it**. The `fraction` is only an approximation Kino keeps for you (and for a progress bar); the exact position belongs in
`resume`.

```js
// Small and exact: the chapter and the page.
await kino.progress.set({ id: manga.id, fraction: 0.4, resume: { cap: 87, pag: 12 } });

// Or the route of your own screen, to open it again just as it was.
await kino.progress.set({ id: book.id, fraction: 0.62, resume: { screen: "reader", args: { book: book.id, at: 18342 } } });
```

- **Keep a margin below 1024.** Kino measures `resume` with the escaping of its JSON library (U+2028 and U+2029 count 6 bytes
  where `JSON.stringify` writes them raw), so a value that `JSON.stringify` measures at exactly 1024 may be refused.
- **Validate what you read back.** Another device wrote it, maybe with another version of your plugin: check its shape before
